bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the positioning accuracy achievable with Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) GNSS surveying under good satellite geometry?
bankQuestions.explanation: RTK uses carrier phase measurements and resolves integer cycle ambiguities in real time, delivering centimeter-level accuracy (1-2 cm horizontal, 2-3 cm vertical).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: RTK GNSS provides 1 to 2 cm horizontal accuracy in real time.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In RTK GNSS surveying, what does "resolving integer carrier phase ambiguity" mean?
options: Determining the exact whole number of carrier wavelengths between the satellite and the receiver antenna at the instant of signal acquisition
bankQuestions.explanation: Carrier phase tracking measures fractional phase precisely, but the initial integer number of complete wavelengths (N) between satellite and antenna is unknown; resolving N is integer ambiguity resolution.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Carrier phase ambiguity resolution finds the whole number of cycles between satellite and antenna.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a CORS network in modern GNSS geodetic infrastructure?
bankQuestions.explanation: CORS stands for Continuously Operating Reference Stations—a permanent network of geodetic GNSS receivers transmitting data to a central server to provide network RTK corrections.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: CORS = Continuously Operating Reference Station network.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What protocol is internationally standardized for streaming real-time GNSS differential corrections over the Internet (cellular network)?
options: NTRIP (Networked Transport of RTCM via Internet Protocol)
bankQuestions.explanation: NTRIP is the standard telecommunication protocol used to stream RTCM differential GNSS corrections over the Internet via cellular mobile data.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: NTRIP transmits RTCM differential GNSS corrections over the Internet/mobile network.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does the term "Multipath error" mean in GNSS positioning?
options: Signals reflecting off surrounding surfaces (buildings, metal roofs, water bodies) before reaching the antenna, causing an artificially longer path length
Receiving signals from multiple satellite constellations
bankQuestions.explanation: Multipath occurs when satellite signals bounce off structures, water, or ground before hitting the receiver antenna, distorting pseudorange and carrier phase measurements.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Multipath error occurs when signals reflect off nearby structures/water before reaching antenna.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which type of GNSS antenna design is specifically engineered to suppress multipath signals arriving from low angles or ground reflections?
bankQuestions.explanation: A choke-ring antenna has concentric metal circular troughs that trap and attenuate reflected signals arriving from below or near the horizon, preventing multipath interference.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Choke-ring antennas suppress ground and low-elevation multipath reflections.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why can ionospheric delay error in GNSS signals be effectively eliminated by dual-frequency (L1 / L2) receivers?
options: Because the ionosphere is a dispersive medium where signal delay is inversely proportional to the square of the frequency (f^2)
Because L2 frequency passes through without delay
Because L1 and L2 have opposite polarities
Because the ionosphere reflects L2 entirely
bankQuestions.explanation: In the ionospheric plasma, refraction delay is dispersive: Δt ∝ 1/f². By measuring the arrival time difference between two distinct frequencies (L1 and L2), ionospheric delay is canceled.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Ionosphere is dispersive (delay ∝ 1/f²); dual-frequency (L1/L2) receivers cancel ionospheric delay.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does the GNSS metric "PDOP" stand for, and what does a low PDOP value signify?
options: Positional Dilution of Precision; a low value signifies excellent satellite spatial geometry and higher positioning accuracy
Phase Difference of Polarization; low value means weak battery
Peak Distance of Orbit; low value means satellite is near
Periodic Drift of Plummet; low value means level tripod
bankQuestions.explanation: PDOP (Positional Dilution of Precision) measures the 3D geometrical distribution of visible satellites. Lower PDOP (e.g., < 3) means satellites are widely dispersed, yielding high accuracy.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: PDOP = Positional Dilution of Precision. Low PDOP (< 4) indicates optimal satellite geometry.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which GNSS surveying method provides the highest absolute geodetic accuracy (millimeter-level) for primary national control networks?
options: Static GNSS surveying with long multi-hour observation sessions
bankQuestions.explanation: Static GNSS surveying records continuous dual-frequency carrier phase data over hours or days for post-processing with precise ephemerides, giving millimeter-level accuracy.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Static GNSS provides the highest precision (2-5 mm) for primary geodetic networks.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In Geographic Information Systems (GIS), what are the two fundamental data structures used to represent geographic features?
options: Vector data model and Raster data model
bankQuestions.explanation: Spatial data in GIS is primarily represented using the Vector model (points, lines, polygons) and the Raster model (regular grid of cells/pixels).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Vector (points, lines, polygons) and Raster (grid cells) are the two primary GIS data models.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which vector geometry type is used in GIS to represent discrete point entities such as survey boundary stones, borewells, or lampposts?
bankQuestions.explanation: A point feature is a zero-dimensional geometric object defined by a single coordinate pair (X, Y) without length or area.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Points represent zero-dimensional locations (wells, survey stones, trees).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which vector geometry type in GIS is used to represent linear features having length but no defined surface area, such as roads, rivers, and contours?
bankQuestions.explanation: Polylines (lines) are one-dimensional features formed by ordered sequences of connected vertices, representing roads, pipelines, rivers, and contour lines.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Polylines represent one-dimensional linear features (roads, streams, contours).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which vector geometry type in GIS is used to represent enclosed spatial features possessing both perimeter and surface area, such as land parcels, lakes, and administrative districts?
bankQuestions.explanation: Polygons are two-dimensional enclosed geographic entities bounded by closed rings of coordinate vertices, used for land parcels, building footprints, and water bodies.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Polygons represent two-dimensional enclosed areas (land parcels, lakes, plots).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS raster data models, what determines the spatial resolution of the dataset?
options: The ground dimension represented by a single raster grid cell (pixel size)
The number of colors in the display palette
The date the image was captured
bankQuestions.explanation: Spatial resolution in a raster dataset is defined by the ground dimension of a single cell (e.g., 30m x 30m cell represents 30-meter resolution).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Raster spatial resolution is determined by the ground cell size (pixel size).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) in GIS?
options: A raster grid representation where each cell value stores the terrain bare-earth elevation above a vertical datum
A vector boundary of river basins
bankQuestions.explanation: A DEM is a raster array of regularly spaced elevation values representing the bare ground topography without vegetation or man-made structures.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: DEM is a raster grid where each cell represents ground surface elevation.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN) in GIS terrain modeling?
options: A vector-based digital terrain model formed by connecting irregular elevation sample points into a network of non-overlapping contiguous triangles
A network of triangulated radio towers
A raster map of mountain shadows
bankQuestions.explanation: A TIN is a vector surface representation composed of irregularly distributed nodes with elevation coordinates connected by edges forming non-overlapping triangles (Delaunay triangulation).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: TIN is a vector-based terrain model composed of contiguous irregular triangles.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Topology" in GIS vector data management?
options: The mathematical expression of spatial relationships (adjacency, connectivity, and containment) between geographic features independent of coordinates
The elevation contour lines of high mountains
The visual color symbology on maps
The speed of network data transfer
bankQuestions.explanation: Topology explicitly defines geometric relationships between vector features: connectivity (arcs connect at nodes), containment (polygons enclose areas), and adjacency (polygons share common boundaries).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Topology defines spatial relationships: connectivity, adjacency, and containment.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Buffering" spatial analysis operation in GIS?
options: Generating a proximity zone of specified distance around point, line, or polygon features
Storing temporary data in computer RAM
bankQuestions.explanation: Buffering creates a new polygon zone around features at a specified buffer distance (e.g., creating a 100-meter protection buffer around a river line).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Buffering creates proximity zones of defined distance around features.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS spatial overlay analysis, what does the "Intersect" operation produce?
options: A new layer containing only the spatial features and attributes that fall within the common overlapping area of both input layers
A layer containing all features from both layers without clipping
The difference between two raster grids
bankQuestions.explanation: Intersect performs a geometric Boolean AND operation: it retains only the geometric regions where both input feature layers overlap, joining their attributes.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Intersect retains only the common overlapping areas of both layers (Boolean AND).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS spatial overlay analysis, what does the "Union" operation produce?
options: A new polygon layer containing all geometric areas and combined attributes from both input layers (Boolean OR)
A single merged table without geometry
bankQuestions.explanation: Union performs a Boolean OR operation on two polygon layers, preserving all features and areas from both inputs, whether overlapping or non-overlapping.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Union combines all areas from both polygon layers (Boolean OR).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the primary difference between Spatial Data and Attribute Data in GIS?
options: Spatial data defines the geographic location, geometry, and shape of features; Attribute data provides descriptive tabular characteristics about those features
Spatial data is stored on paper while attribute data is digital
Spatial data contains only text while attribute data contains graphics
bankQuestions.explanation: Spatial data represents geographic position and geometric form (where it is); Attribute data consists of descriptive facts, properties, and values stored in tables (what it is).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Spatial data = WHERE (geometry/coordinates). Attribute data = WHAT (tabular characteristics).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the standard global reference ellipsoid and geodetic datum used by the GPS system and modern worldwide GIS datasets?
bankQuestions.explanation: WGS 84 is the global geocentric reference ellipsoid and datum developed by the US Department of Defense, utilized as the native coordinate reference system for GPS.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: WGS 84 is the standard global geodetic datum used by GPS.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) coordinate system, how many longitudinal zones is the entire globe divided into?
bankQuestions.explanation: The UTM system divides the world between 80°S and 84°N into 60 longitudinal zones, each spanning 6° of longitude, numbered 1 to 60 starting at the 180° meridian moving eastward.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: UTM divides the world into 60 zones, each 6° longitude wide.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the scale factor assigned along the Central Meridian in each UTM projection zone to minimize scale distortion across the zone?
bankQuestions.explanation: To balance scale distortion across the 6° width of the zone, the UTM secant projection sets the scale factor at the Central Meridian to exactly 0.9996.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: UTM central meridian scale factor is exactly 0.9996.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the False Easting assigned to the Central Meridian in every UTM zone to avoid negative coordinate values?
bankQuestions.explanation: To ensure all easting coordinates within a zone remain positive numbers, the Central Meridian is arbitrarily assigned a False Easting of 500,000 meters.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: False Easting of UTM central meridian = 500,000 m.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the primary objective of Hydrographic Surveying?
options: Mapping water bodies to determine bed topography, water depths, shorelines, and underwater navigation hazards for nautical charts and marine works
bankQuestions.explanation: Hydrographic surveying surveys water bodies (oceans, seas, lakes, rivers) to map depth of water, seabed contours, navigational channels, and marine construction sites.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Hydrographic surveying maps underwater bed relief and depths for navigation and harbor works.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the operation of measuring the vertical depth of the water bed below the water surface called in hydrography?
bankQuestions.explanation: Sounding is the measurement of depth of water below the water surface at various points in a body of water.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sounding = measuring depth of water from the water surface to the bed.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Up to what water depth is a graduated sounding pole (sounding rod) typically recommended for taking depth measurements?
bankQuestions.explanation: Sounding poles are wooden poles 5 to 6 meters long, graduated in decimeters, used in shallow, calm waters where lead lines would drift.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sounding pole is used in shallow waters up to 5 to 6 meters depth.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is provided at the bottom of the lead weight of a sounding lead line to collect samples of the seabed material?
options: A hollow conical cavity filled with tallow or beeswax (arming the lead)
bankQuestions.explanation: The base of the lead weight has a cup-shaped recess filled with tallow or wax ("arming"). When the lead strikes the bottom, sand, mud, or shells stick to the tallow for sampling.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Arming the lead: cavity filled with tallow collects seabed material samples.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the operating principle of an Echo Sounder (Fathometer) used for hydrographic soundings?
options: Emitting acoustic sound pulses downwards and measuring the two-way travel time reflected from the seabed: depth = (v * t) / 2
Measuring radio wave reflection from clouds
Measuring water pressure at the sea surface
Using laser beams through opaque muddy water
bankQuestions.explanation: An echo sounder emits ultrasonic sound pulses through an electroacoustic transducer and measures the round-trip time t: d = (v * t) / 2, where v is the speed of sound in water (~1460 to 1500 m/s).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Echo sounder / Fathometer: Depth = (v x t) / 2 using acoustic sound pulses.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the average velocity of sound in seawater used for hydrographic echo sounding computations?
bankQuestions.explanation: The speed of sound in seawater is roughly 1,500 m/s (compared to ~343 m/s in air), varying slightly with salinity, temperature, and depth.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Speed of sound in seawater is ~1,500 m/s (in freshwater ~1,460 m/s).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: When do Spring Tides occur in nature?
options: At the times of New Moon and Full Moon, when the Sun, Moon, and Earth align in a straight line (syzygy)
At the first and third quarters of the Moon
Only during spring equinox in March
When the Moon is at its greatest distance from Earth
bankQuestions.explanation: Spring tides occur twice each lunar month during New Moon and Full Moon (syzygy), when the gravitational pulls of the Sun and Moon reinforce each other, producing maximum tidal range.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Spring tides occur at New Moon and Full Moon (maximum tidal range).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: When do Neap Tides occur in nature?
options: At the first and third quarters of the Moon (quadrature), when the Sun and Moon gravitational forces act at right angles
bankQuestions.explanation: Neap tides occur during the Moon first and third quarters (quadrature), when the solar and lunar tides oppose each other at right angles, causing the lowest tidal range (least high tides, highest low tides).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Neap tides occur at Moon first/third quarter (minimum tidal range).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the standard vertical reference datum adopted internationally on navigational nautical charts for recording soundings?
options: Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT) or Chart Datum
bankQuestions.explanation: Chart Datum is usually set to Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT) so that navigators are assured that the actual depth of water will almost never be less than the chartered depth.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Soundings on nautical charts are referenced to Chart Datum / Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What instrument is used by an observer on a moving survey boat to measure horizontal angles between shore signals for fixing the sounding location?
bankQuestions.explanation: A nautical sextant can be held and read in the hands without requiring a stable tripod, enabling instantaneous measurement of angles between shore objects from a rolling boat.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Nautical sextant is used to observe horizontal angles from a moving survey boat.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: On what optical principle does a Nautical Sextant function?
options: Principle of double reflection: the angle between the first incident ray and last reflected ray is twice the angle between the two mirrors
Principle of refraction through optical prisms
Principle of total internal reflection in fiber glass
bankQuestions.explanation: A sextant has two mirrors: the index mirror and the horizon mirror. By the law of double reflection, when a ray is reflected successively from two mirrors, the angle of deviation is twice the angle between the mirrors.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sextant principle: angle between incident and reflected ray is TWICE the angle between mirrors.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In hydrographic surveying, what is the "Three-Point Problem"?
options: Locating the position of a sounding boat by measuring two horizontal angles between three known shore stations
Locating three points with a theodolite
Setting up a tripod on three legs
Measuring the volume of three dredging cuts
bankQuestions.explanation: The three-point problem involves determining the position of an unknown boat station P by observing two horizontal angles α and β subtended by three visible shore stations (A, B, C) of known coordinates.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Three-Point Problem: locating boat position from 2 angles observed to 3 known shore points.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which mechanical drafting instrument is specially designed to plot the solution of the Three-Point Problem on hydrographic survey sheets?
bankQuestions.explanation: A station pointer consists of a graduated circle with one fixed central arm and two movable arms. The two measured angles are set on the arms and the instrument is positioned until all three arms pass through the shore points.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Station pointer (three-arm protractor) mechanically plots the Three-Point Problem.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What condition causes the solution of the Three-Point Problem to become indeterminate (the danger circle condition)?
options: When the boat position P lies on the circumference of the circle passing through the three shore control stations A, B, and C
When the boat is closer than 10 meters to shore
When the water depth exceeds 50 meters
When the tide is at spring tide
bankQuestions.explanation: If the boat position lies on the great circle passing through the three shore stations (A, B, C), the geometry becomes mathematically indeterminate because any point on that circle subtends the exact same angles.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Indeterminate condition (danger circle): boat lies on the circle passing through the 3 shore points.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which instrument is commonly used to measure water flow velocity in open river streams for discharge calculations?
options: Current meter (e.g., Price current meter or Ott propeller meter)
bankQuestions.explanation: A current meter has a rotating wheel of conical cups (Price) or a helical propeller (Ott) that rotates at a speed proportional to the velocity of water flow.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Current meter (Price / Ott) measures stream flow velocity in rivers.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In stream gauging, at what depth below the water surface is the single-point velocity observation taken to represent mean stream velocity?
options: 0.6 of the total depth (measured from the water surface)
bankQuestions.explanation: Extensive stream gauging research proves that the velocity at 0.6 of depth from the surface closely approximates the mean velocity in the vertical velocity profile.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Single-point velocity measurement: observed at 0.6 depth from surface.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: When the two-point method is used to determine mean velocity in a deep river stream, at what depths are the velocity observations taken?
options: At 0.2 depth and 0.8 depth, and the two values are averaged: V_mean = (V_0.2 + V_0.8) / 2
bankQuestions.explanation: In the two-point method, velocities are measured at 0.2 and 0.8 of the depth below the surface. The mean velocity is the arithmetic average: V_mean = 0.5 * (V_0.2 + V_0.8).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Two-point method: V_mean = (V_0.2 + V_0.8) / 2.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In Total Station surveying, what is the "forced centering" (three-tripod) technique?
options: Interchanging the instrument and target prisms onto fixed tribrachs on tripods without disturbing tripod legs, eliminating station centering errors
Forcing the tripod legs deeper into soil with a mallet
Centering the bubble using only two footscrews
Locking the horizontal clamp with excessive torque
bankQuestions.explanation: In forced centering, tribrachs remain undisturbed on tripods over survey marks; only the Total Station and prisms are swapped between tribrachs, eliminating intermediate centering errors in traverses.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Forced centering interchanges instrument and prisms on fixed tribrachs, eliminating centering errors.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the function of the laser plummet in modern electronic Total Stations?
options: Emitting a focused visible red laser beam vertically downward through the vertical axis to mark the ground station peg directly
Measuring distance to overhead power cables
Guiding the surveyor during night driving
Aligning the line of collimation with true north
bankQuestions.explanation: A laser plummet projects a small visible red laser dot straight down through the vertical axis of the tribrach, allowing instant visual centering over the ground mark without looking through an eyepiece.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Laser plummet projects a vertical red laser dot onto the ground mark for fast centering.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What type of staff is used with a high-precision Digital Electronic Level to take automatic height readings?
options: An Invar staff carrying a printed barcode pattern
An ordinary wooden folding staff graduated in centimeters
A telescopic aluminum staff with red and black numerals
bankQuestions.explanation: Digital levels utilize barcode staves (often made of invar for thermal stability). An internal CCD sensor scans the barcode pattern and calculates elevation and distance automatically.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Digital levels use barcode staves (scanned by internal CCD line sensors).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which eye safety laser hazard classification applies to the visible aiming laser diodes used in reflectorless Total Stations?
bankQuestions.explanation: Visible lasers in surveying are typically Class 2 (<1 mW, safe for accidental blink reflex <0.25 s) or Class 3R (up to 5 mW, direct intrabeam viewing is hazardous).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Surveying lasers are Class 2 (<1 mW) or Class 3R (<5 mW).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In Total Station angle measurement, what is an absolute rotary encoder?
options: A coded glass disk with patterned tracks where each angular position has a unique binary digital code that is instantly read upon power-on without indexing
A mechanical gear train that counts revolutions
A liquid vial with electronic electrodes
A magnetic needle that senses magnetic north
bankQuestions.explanation: An absolute encoder uses glass disks with binary optical code patterns (such as Gray code); the instrument reads the exact absolute angle immediately upon powering up without needing a 360° spin.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Absolute encoders read exact angular positions immediately from uniquely coded glass disks.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the standard LandXML data format used for in modern survey and civil engineering software?
options: An XML-based standard file format for exchanging survey points, alignments, parcel boundaries, surfaces, and cross-sections between CAD and GIS applications
A device driver for battery chargers
bankQuestions.explanation: LandXML is an open, non-proprietary XML data schema used industry-wide to exchange civil engineering and survey measurement data (surfaces, alignments, parcels, points).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: LandXML is the open XML schema for exchanging survey points, surfaces, and alignments.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the 360-degree prism used in robotic Total Station surveying?
options: It reflects the EDM beam back to the instrument from any horizontal direction without needing to be oriented towards the instrument
It measures angles in all 360 degrees simultaneously
It eliminates the need for tripod leveling
bankQuestions.explanation: A 360-degree prism comprises six joined corner-cube prisms arranged in a ring, ensuring the robotic tracker maintains lock from any direction as the surveyor walks.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: 360° prism reflects EDM signals from any direction, ideal for robotic rover tracking.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GNSS signal processing, what is a "cycle slip"?
options: A sudden discontinuity or loss of integer lock in the carrier phase count caused by temporary physical obstruction of the satellite signal
A mechanical slip in the tripod head clamp
A discrepancy between local time and UTC
A calculation error in coordinate transformation
bankQuestions.explanation: A cycle slip occurs when tree leaves, buildings, or intense ionospheric scintillation temporarily block a satellite signal, causing the receiver to lose track of the integer number of wavelengths.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Cycle slip = sudden loss of lock on carrier phase integer cycle count due to obstruction.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the GNSS "Double Difference" mathematical observable in baseline processing?
options: It eliminates both satellite clock bias and receiver clock bias simultaneously
bankQuestions.explanation: By differencing observations between two receivers and two satellites, both the satellite clock errors and receiver clock errors cancel out completely.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Double differencing eliminates BOTH satellite clock error and receiver clock error.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does the GNSS observable "Triple Difference" eliminate in baseline post-processing?
options: The integer carrier phase ambiguity (N), making it ideal for detecting cycle slips
bankQuestions.explanation: Differencing double differences across two consecutive time epochs cancels out the constant integer ambiguity N, allowing rapid detection and repair of cycle slips.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Triple differencing cancels integer ambiguity N, used to detect cycle slips.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is Precise Point Positioning (PPP) in GNSS technology?
options: A positioning method providing decimeter-to-centimeter accuracy for a single standalone GNSS receiver using precise satellite orbits and clock products without a local base station
Setting a theodolite over an exact survey mark
Using four rovers connected by wires
A manual plotting method on topo sheets
bankQuestions.explanation: PPP uses dual-frequency carrier phase and pseudorange data from a single receiver combined with precise satellite clock corrections and orbits (from IGS) to compute accurate coordinates without a reference station.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: PPP delivers high-accuracy positioning for a single receiver without a local base station.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the International GNSS Service (IGS)?
options: A voluntary global federation providing high-precision GNSS satellite orbits, clock corrections, and Earth rotation parameters for scientific and surveying applications
A commercial company selling satellite hardware
A military surveillance wing of NATO
An agency providing international marine charts
bankQuestions.explanation: The IGS is a global federation of tracking stations and analysis centers that makes open-access precise orbits, satellite clock data, and atmospheric products available worldwide.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: IGS provides open-access precise satellite orbits and clock corrections globally.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a Virtual Reference Station (VRS) in network RTK surveying?
options: An imaginary reference station mathematically created by central network software near the rover position to broadcast customized local RTK corrections
A physical concrete pillar erected on mountain tops
A satellite stationed directly above the surveyor
A computer simulator for student training
bankQuestions.explanation: In a VRS network, the rover sends its approximate position via NTRIP; the central server calculates synthetic base station corrections for an imaginary station right next to the rover.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: VRS is a synthetic virtual base station generated by network software close to the rover.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the GPS Time (GPST) reference standard and how does it relate to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)?
options: GPST is a continuous atomic time scale that does NOT insert leap seconds, differing from UTC by an integer number of leap seconds
GPST is identical to Greenwich Mean Time in every respect
GPST changes with local daylight saving time
GPST resets to zero at the start of every calendar year
bankQuestions.explanation: GPST began at 00:00:00 UTC on January 6, 1980. Unlike UTC, GPST does not insert leap seconds, so GPST is currently ahead of UTC by an exact integer number of leap seconds (e.g. 18 seconds).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: GPS Time is continuous without leap seconds; differs from UTC by integer leap seconds.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How long is one GPS Navigation Message frame, and at what bit rate is it transmitted by the satellites?
options: 1500 bits transmitted at a data rate of 50 bits per second (30 seconds per frame)
bankQuestions.explanation: A complete GPS navigation message frame has 1,500 bits divided into five 300-bit subframes, transmitted at 50 bps, taking exactly 30 seconds per frame.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: GPS navigation message frame = 1500 bits at 50 bps (takes 30 seconds).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What critical orbital data is broadcast in Subframes 2 and 3 of the GPS Navigation Message?
options: Broadcast Ephemeris (precise parameters defining the satellite Keplerian orbit)
bankQuestions.explanation: Subframes 2 and 3 contain the broadcast ephemeris parameters representing the Keplerian orbital elements of the transmitting satellite, valid for roughly 2 to 4 hours.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Subframes 2 & 3 carry the broadcast ephemeris (precise orbit of the transmitting satellite).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the GPS Almanac data transmitted in Subframes 4 and 5 of the navigation message?
options: Coarse orbital and status information for ALL operational satellites in the constellation, helping receivers locate satellites quickly upon power-on
Weather forecasts across ground tracking stations
bankQuestions.explanation: The almanac contains rough orbital parameters for all constellation satellites, allowing a receiver to determine which satellites are above the local horizon during warm starts.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Almanac provides rough orbital data for ALL satellites to enable fast acquisition.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "elevation mask angle" (cutoff angle) typically set in a GNSS survey receiver, and why is it used?
options: 10 to 15 degrees above the horizon, to ignore satellites with low elevation angles suffering from severe atmospheric delay and multipath
45 degrees, to view only zenith satellites
0 degrees, to capture signals down to the ground
90 degrees, to track one satellite overhead
bankQuestions.explanation: Signals from satellites below 10°–15° travel through very thick layers of troposphere and ionosphere and are prone to multipath. A mask angle rejects them to protect survey accuracy.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Elevation mask (10°–15°) rejects low-altitude satellites subject to high atmospheric noise.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the difference between Geodetic Height (h), Orthometric Height (H), and Geoid Undulation (N)?
options: Geodetic height h (above the WGS84 ellipsoid) equals Orthometric height H (above MSL geoid) plus Geoid undulation N: h = H + N
bankQuestions.explanation: GPS measures ellipsoidal height h directly. True elevation above mean sea level is orthometric height H, related by the geoid separation N: h = H + N (or H = h - N).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Fundamental height relationship: h (ellipsoidal) = H (orthometric/MSL) + N (geoid).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Geoid in physical geodesy?
options: The equipotential surface of the Earth gravity field that best coincides with global Mean Sea Level in the absence of tides and currents
A smooth mathematical reference oblate spheroid
The actual topography of mountains and valleys
The outer boundary of the atmosphere
bankQuestions.explanation: The geoid is an equipotential surface of the Earth gravity potential field to which the plumb line is everywhere perpendicular, serving as the datum for orthometric elevations.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Geoid is the equipotential gravity surface that coincides with undisturbed Mean Sea Level.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In remote sensing, what is the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) formula calculated from satellite bands?
bankQuestions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red light strongly while spongy mesophyll reflects near-infrared (NIR). NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red) quantifies live green vegetation.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red). Ranges from -1.0 to +1.0.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What range of NDVI values typically indicates dense, healthy, green agricultural crops or tropical rainforest canopy?
bankQuestions.explanation: Healthy green vegetation exhibits high NIR reflection and low red reflection, giving NDVI values between 0.6 and 0.9. Bare soil is 0.1 to 0.2, and water gives negative values.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Dense green vegetation gives NDVI between 0.6 and 0.9. Water is negative.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What are the four primary sensor resolutions that define the capabilities of a remote sensing satellite system?
options: Spatial resolution, Spectral resolution, Radiometric resolution, and Temporal resolution
Focal length, aperture, shutter speed, and ISO
Red, green, blue, and near infrared
bankQuestions.explanation: The four fundamental resolutions of remote sensing are Spatial (pixel size), Spectral (band wavelength interval), Radiometric (bit depth sensitivity), and Temporal (revisit cycle).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Four remote sensing resolutions: Spatial, Spectral, Radiometric, and Temporal.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is Radiometric Resolution in satellite imaging systems?
options: The sensitivity of the sensor to detect subtle differences in electromagnetic energy, represented by the number of bits per pixel (e.g., 8-bit, 12-bit, 16-bit)
The physical width of a pixel in meters
The number of spectral bands on the sensor
The speed at which the satellite orbits Earth
bankQuestions.explanation: Radiometric resolution is measured in bits: an 8-bit sensor records 256 gray levels (0-255), while an 11-bit sensor records 2048 levels, providing higher contrast sensitivity.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Radiometric resolution is the sensor energy sensitivity measured in bit depth (e.g. 8-bit, 12-bit).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In remote sensing, which portion of the electromagnetic spectrum is called the "Thermal Infrared" (TIR) region, utilized to map surface temperatures?
bankQuestions.explanation: The thermal infrared band spans roughly 8 to 14 μm, where terrestrial objects emit radiant heat energy according to their thermodynamic temperature.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Thermal infrared band (8 - 14 μm) senses emitted heat for surface temperature mapping.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is an "Orthophoto" (or ortho-rectified aerial image)?
options: An aerial photograph or satellite image geometrically corrected for terrain relief displacement, camera tilt, and optical distortion so it possesses a uniform map scale
An unedited oblique aerial photograph taken from an airplane window
A photograph taken in infrared light only
bankQuestions.explanation: Orthorectification removes perspective distortion and elevation displacement using a DEM, turning the photograph into a planimetrically true map with uniform scale throughout.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Orthophoto is an aerial image corrected for terrain relief and tilt to have uniform map scale.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which file format standard consists of a collection of files with extensions .shp, .shx, .dbf, and .prj, widely used in GIS vector mapping?
bankQuestions.explanation: An ESRI Shapefile uses .shp for feature geometry, .shx for spatial indexing, .dbf for attribute dBASE tables, and .prj for coordinate system projection information.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Shapefile suite: .shp (geometry), .shx (index), .dbf (attributes), .prj (projection).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the GIS spatial analysis function "Clip" used for?
options: Cutting out a specific geographic region of an input layer using the boundary of another polygon layer as a cookie cutter
Deleting duplicate records in an attribute table
Converting raster pixels into vector lines
bankQuestions.explanation: Clip acts like a cookie cutter: it extracts spatial features from an input layer that fall strictly inside the boundary of a defined clip polygon layer without combining attributes.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Clip extracts features from an input layer using a bounding polygon as a cookie-cutter.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS database management, what is a "Primary Key"?
options: A unique attribute field (such as FID or Parcel_ID) that uniquely identifies each individual feature or record in a table
The password to open an encrypted shapefile
The coordinate value of the origin point
bankQuestions.explanation: A primary key is an attribute column containing strictly unique values for every row in a table, ensuring each geographic feature can be identified and linked to other tables.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Primary key is a unique identifier (e.g. FID, PIN) for each feature in a GIS table.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS map projections, what does a "Conformal" map projection preserve accurately?
options: Local angles and shapes of small geographic features
The true areas of all landmasses
True scale in all directions across the entire map
Straight lines for all compass headings
bankQuestions.explanation: A conformal (orthomorphic) projection preserves angular relationships around any point, meaning local shapes are rendered correctly without angular deformation.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Conformal projection preserves local shapes and angles (e.g. Mercator, Lambert Conformal).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS map projections, what does an "Equivalent" (Equal-Area) map projection preserve accurately?
options: The relative surface areas of geographic regions throughout the map
The true shapes of small islands
bankQuestions.explanation: An equal-area (equivalent) projection maintains the proportional area of any region on the map equal to its true area on the globe, though shapes may be distorted.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Equivalent (equal-area) projections preserve true areas across the map.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which map projection is standardly used for topographic mapping of regions with large East-West extents, such as the United States or Mediterranean Europe?
bankQuestions.explanation: The Lambert Conformal Conic projection uses a secant cone, minimizing distortion along two standard parallels, making it ideal for mid-latitude zones extending East-West.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Lambert Conformal Conic is ideal for mid-latitude regions with East-West elongation.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a Multibeam Echo Sounder (MBES) and how does it differ from a single-beam echo sounder?
options: It transmits a wide fan-shaped swath of acoustic beams across the seafloor, providing 100% full bottom bathymetric coverage in a single survey pass
It operates using laser light instead of acoustic sound
It measures soundings only directly underneath the boat keel
It requires three boats operating together
bankQuestions.explanation: An MBES projects a fan-shaped acoustic swath across the track, collecting hundreds of individual depth soundings simultaneously to generate high-resolution bathymetric surfaces.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Multibeam echo sounder (MBES) emits a fan of acoustic beams for 100% bottom coverage.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is Side Scan Sonar (SSS) used for in hydrographic marine exploration?
options: Producing detailed photographic-like acoustic imagery of the seabed to detect shipwrecks, exposed pipelines, boulders, and bottom texture
Measuring water salinity at the river mouth
Drilling core samples into rock strata
bankQuestions.explanation: Side Scan Sonar sends conical or fan-shaped sound pulses sideways toward the seabed and measures backscatter amplitude, creating photo-quality images of seafloor features.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Side Scan Sonar produces acoustic imagery of seabed textures, pipelines, and submerged wrecks.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In hydrographic surveying, what are "Cross Lines" (check lines) and why are they run?
options: Sounding lines run perpendicular to the principal sounding lines at regular intervals to verify depth measurement repeatability and tidal reduction accuracy
Boundary survey lines on dry land
Cables laid across a river to guide ferry boats
bankQuestions.explanation: Cross lines are sounding lines surveyed roughly orthogonal to the main survey lines (typically at 10 to 15 times the line spacing) to cross-check depth soundings at intersections.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Cross lines run perpendicular to main sounding lines to independently check sounding accuracy.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why must a sounding lead line be thoroughly wetted and soaked in water prior to graduating and using it in field surveys?
options: Because hemp and cotton lines shrink significantly when immersed in water, which would cause large systematic depth measurement errors if graduated dry
To make the line sink faster
To make the line visible underwater
bankQuestions.explanation: Natural hemp or cord lines shrink substantially when wet. They must be pre-soaked and stretched under working loads before graduation marks are applied.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sounding lines shrink when wet; must be soaked and stretched before graduation.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Stilling Well" used for in an automatic float-type tide gauge installation?
options: Damping out short-period surface waves and boat wakes so the float records true gradual tidal oscillations accurately
Storing drinking water on the survey vessel
Preventing fish from touching the sensor
bankQuestions.explanation: A stilling well is a vertical pipe connected to the sea via a small bottom orifice. High-frequency wind waves are filtered out, while low-frequency tidal changes enter smoothly.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Stilling well damps high-frequency surface waves to measure true tidal levels.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the full period of the Metonic cycle of lunar tidal variations, required for establishing an absolute Mean Sea Level datum from tide gauge records?
options: 19 years (specifically 18.6 years for lunar node regression)
bankQuestions.explanation: To average out all astronomical tidal cycles (including the 18.6-year nodal cycle of the Moon orbit), continuous hourly tidal observations over 19 years are standardly required.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: A complete tidal datum observation cycle is 19 years (18.6-year lunar nodal cycle).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Italian method" (analytical method) in solving the hydrographic Three-Point Problem?
options: An analytical mathematical procedure using trigonometric formulas to compute the coordinates of the boat station from the measured horizontal angles
A graphic method using three needles on tracing paper
An optical sighting instrument with two prisms
A manual plotting method using drafting triangles
bankQuestions.explanation: The Italian method is a rigorous analytical trigonometric solution that sets up coordinate equations based on circumscribing circles to solve for station coordinates.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Italian method is an analytical trigonometric solution to the Three-Point Problem.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In hydrographic soundings, what is "Tidal Reduction"?
options: The mathematical correction subtracted from observed sounding depths to reduce them to the designated Chart Datum based on simultaneous tide gauge readings
The decrease in water depth during low tide
The erosion of beaches by tidal currents
The loss of sound signal in deep ocean trenches
bankQuestions.explanation: Soundings are measured from the instantaneous water level. Subtracting the height of tide above Chart Datum at that precise minute gives the standardized charted depth.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Tidal reduction subtracts the instantaneous tide height to refer depths to Chart Datum.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Sub-bottom Profiler" used for in marine hydrographic and geophysical surveys?
options: Emitting low-frequency acoustic energy to penetrate below the seafloor and image the underlying geological sediment and bedrock stratigraphy
Measuring water temperature at the surface
Measuring wind speed over open ocean
bankQuestions.explanation: Sub-bottom profilers emit low-frequency sound pulses (e.g., 0.5 to 12 kHz) that penetrate sediment layers, reflecting off sub-surface boundaries to image sediment layering.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sub-bottom profilers use low-frequency acoustics to map sediment layers beneath the seabed.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of "Sounding Ranges" (transit lines marked by range beacons on shore)?
options: Keeping the sounding boat on a straight, pre-determined survey course by aligning two prominent shore beacons in a line of sight
Measuring the maximum distance a boat can travel on fuel
Setting the radio frequency for telemetry
Marking high-water flood levels on riverbanks
bankQuestions.explanation: Sounding ranges are straight lines established on the water by pairs of shore range beacons (front and rear). The boat steers so the two beacons stay aligned in sight.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sounding ranges guide the survey boat along straight designated profile lines.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In hydrographic soundings, what is the "lead line" constructed from to minimize elasticity and stretching under working water loads?
options: Well-seasoned, pre-stretched braided hemp or cotton cord with a brass wire core
bankQuestions.explanation: Lead lines are made of high-quality braided hemp or cotton rope, often reinforced with an internal phosphor bronze or brass wire core to prevent stretching.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Lead lines use pre-stretched braided hemp cord with wire core to prevent stretching.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the standard weight of the lead sinker attached to a boat lead line used for shallow coastal soundings?
bankQuestions.explanation: For ordinary coastal and harbour soundings, lead sinkers weigh between 3 kg and 5 kg (7 to 10 lbs) to descend rapidly through moving water currents without excessive weight for the leadsman.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Lead sinkers for harbour soundings weigh 3 to 5 kg (7 to 10 lbs).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of conducting a "Bar Check" on an echo sounder before and after a hydrographic survey mission?
options: Calibrating the sound velocity setting and zero draft index of the acoustic transducer by lowering a metal plate to known measured depths beneath the boat
Checking the boat engine fuel level
Cleaning marine barnacles from the hull
bankQuestions.explanation: A bar check lowers a steel plate on calibrated lines beneath the transducer at known depth intervals (e.g. 2m, 5m, 10m) to calibrate the speed of sound setting and draft offset.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Bar check calibrates sound velocity and transducer draft index of an echo sounder.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In hydrographic surveys of wide estuaries, which method of locating sounding positions is most suitable when strong tidal currents make keeping a boat on a range difficult?
options: Two horizontal theodolite angles observed simultaneously from two synchronized shore base stations
Sounding by pacing along the beach
Using a hand level from the boat
Relying on dead reckoning without sights
bankQuestions.explanation: When currents push the boat off course, observers at two shore stations with theodolites simultaneously sight the boat mast upon a radio/flag signal, plotting its position by intersection.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Two theodolite angles from shore stations locate boats accurately even in strong drift currents.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Current Pole" used for in hydrographic river surveys?
options: Measuring the surface velocity and direction of water flow currents
Measuring the electrical charge of sea water
bankQuestions.explanation: A current pole is a weighted wooden pole floating vertically with a small portion exposed, paid out on a graduated log line to measure current speed and direction.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Current pole measures the surface drift velocity and current direction in rivers/harbours.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In hydrographic surveying, what does "Chart Datum" coincide with along the coasts of India as established by the Naval Hydrographic Office?
options: Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT) or approximately Indian Spring Low Water
The ground surface level of Mumbai port
bankQuestions.explanation: Chart Datum on Indian hydrographic charts is established at Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT) or Indian Spring Low Water (ISLW), below which water rarely falls.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Chart Datum in India is referenced to Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT) / Indian Spring Low Water.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is an "Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler" (ADCP) used for in modern oceanographic surveying?
options: Measuring water velocity profiles across the entire water column depth using Doppler frequency shifts of acoustic sound reflected from suspended particles
bankQuestions.explanation: ADCP transmits ultrasonic sound pulses and measures the Doppler frequency shift reflected from microscopic particles, computing flow velocity at multiple depth layers.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: ADCP measures complete water current velocity profiles using acoustic Doppler shifts.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the definition of "Tidal Range" in oceanography?
options: The vertical difference in height between consecutive high tide and low tide levels
The horizontal distance between the high tide mark and low tide mark on a beach
The time elapsed between two high tides
The speed of tidal flood currents
bankQuestions.explanation: Tidal range is the vertical difference in water elevation between a high tide crest and its preceding or succeeding low tide trough.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Tidal range = vertical difference between High Water and Low Water levels.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Diurnal Tide"?
options: A tidal pattern consisting of only ONE high tide and ONE low tide in each lunar day of approximately 24 hours and 50 minutes
A tide that occurs twice every 12 hours
A tide that occurs only during daylight hours
A tide caused by underwater volcanic eruptions
bankQuestions.explanation: A diurnal tide has one high water and one low water each lunar day (~24.84 hours). In contrast, semidiurnal tides have two highs and two lows each day.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Diurnal tide: ONE high tide and ONE low tide per lunar day.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Semidiurnal Tide"?
options: A tidal pattern featuring TWO high tides and TWO low tides of approximately equal heights in each lunar day
A tide occurring once every six months
A tide that occurs only at night
bankQuestions.explanation: Semidiurnal tides feature two high waters and two low waters of roughly similar heights within each lunar day (~12 hours and 25 minutes between successive high tides).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Semidiurnal tide: TWO high tides and TWO low tides of similar height per lunar day.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In Total Station prism measurements, why is the constant offset of a standard Leica round prism designated as 0 mm whereas for third-party universal mounts it is -34 mm?
options: Leica defines the mount mechanical offset so the effective constant is zeroed in the instrument hardware default setting
Third party prisms have convex mirrors
Because light travels faster in Swiss glass
bankQuestions.explanation: Leica calibrates its instrument firmware to treat its proprietary prism geometry as 0 mm offset, whereas universal standard prisms require entering -30 mm or -34 mm.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Leica system defines its standard prism as 0 mm; universal prisms typically enter -30 mm or -34 mm.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the function of the "Electronic Circular Bubble" displayed on the LCD graphic screen of modern Total Stations?
options: Displaying real-time graphic bubble leveling derived from the dual-axis tilt sensor for fast, precise instrument leveling without parallax
bankQuestions.explanation: Modern Total Stations display an electronic graphic bullseye bubble on screen with real-time numeric tilt values in seconds of arc, replacing physical bubble estimation.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Electronic bubble uses internal tilt sensors to display precise leveling status on the LCD screen.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In EDM distance calculation, how does an increase in atmospheric temperature affect the velocity of light in air?
options: Warmer air is less dense, so the refractive index decreases and the speed of light increases slightly
Warmer air stops light transmission completely
Temperature has zero effect on electromagnetic velocity
bankQuestions.explanation: As air temperature rises, air expands and becomes less dense. Its refractive index n decreases toward 1.0, causing electromagnetic wave velocity (v = c/n) to increase.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Higher temperature reduces air density, decreasing refractive index and increasing light velocity.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In EDM distance calculation, how does an increase in barometric atmospheric pressure affect the velocity of light in air?
options: Higher pressure increases air density, which increases the refractive index and decreases the speed of light
Higher pressure causes light to travel faster
Higher pressure converts light into heat
Pressure has no physical effect on air density
bankQuestions.explanation: Higher barometric pressure packs more air molecules per unit volume, increasing density and refractive index n, thereby slowing down light waves.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Higher barometric pressure increases air density, slowing down light wave velocity.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the typical least count of the electronic angle reading system in a standard 1-second total station?
bankQuestions.explanation: High-precision engineering Total Stations feature electronic angle resolution of 1 second (1") or 0.1 second (0.1") of arc.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Modern high-precision total stations provide angular display resolutions down to 1" or 0.5".
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the "Base-Rover" radio communication link in Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) GNSS surveying?
options: Transmitting real-time RTCM differential phase correction messages from the reference base receiver to the roving receiver
Streaming video from the rod camera
bankQuestions.explanation: The UHF radio or cellular link transmits standardized RTCM correction packets containing raw satellite carrier phase data from the base to the rover every second.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: UHF radio/cellular link streams RTCM carrier phase corrections from Base to Rover in real time.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does "RTCM" stand for in GNSS differential correction broadcasting?
options: Radio Technical Commission for Maritime Services
bankQuestions.explanation: RTCM (Radio Technical Commission for Maritime Services) develops international open standards (such as RTCM 10403 for RTK) for differential GNSS correction messages.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: RTCM = Radio Technical Commission for Maritime Services (standard format for DGPS/RTK).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GNSS positioning, what is "Autonomous Positioning"?
options: Single-point standalone positioning using only satellite broadcast signals received by a single isolated receiver without any differential corrections
Positioning guided by an inertial submarine gyro
Robotic pole tracking without a surveyor
bankQuestions.explanation: Autonomous positioning (or Single Point Positioning - SPP) computes coordinates using standard broadcast pseudoranges from a single receiver, delivering typical accuracies of 3 to 10 m.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Autonomous positioning = single standalone receiver positioning without differential corrections.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the difference between active and passive remote sensing systems?
options: Active sensors emit their own electromagnetic radiation to illuminate targets (e.g., Radar, LiDAR), whereas passive sensors measure reflected or emitted natural sunlight/heat (e.g., optical cameras, multispectral scanners)
Active sensors move continuously while passive sensors stay still
Active sensors use batteries while passive sensors use solar cells
Active sensors operate underwater while passive sensors operate in air
bankQuestions.explanation: Active sensors (Radar, LiDAR) provide their own illumination source. Passive sensors (optical cameras, Landsat, Sentinel-2) record reflected solar radiation or emitted thermal energy.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Active sensors supply their own energy (LiDAR/Radar); Passive sensors detect natural solar/thermal energy.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is LiDAR in aerial and terrestrial surveying?
options: Light Detection and Ranging: an active optical remote sensing system that pulses laser beams to measure high-density 3D surface coordinates
Liquid Displacement Ranging for depth sounding
bankQuestions.explanation: LiDAR fires hundreds of thousands of laser pulses per second, measuring return time to generate ultra-dense 3D point clouds of terrain, vegetation, and infrastructure.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: LiDAR = Light Detection and Ranging (pulses laser beams to generate dense 3D point clouds).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GIS, what is the spatial operation "Dissolve" used for?
options: Aggregating and merging adjacent polygons that share the same specified attribute value into a single combined boundary
bankQuestions.explanation: Dissolve combines adjacent contiguous polygons having identical attribute values (e.g. merging individual village parcels sharing the same "District" name into a unified district polygon).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Dissolve merges adjacent polygons sharing the same attribute value into a single polygon.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Spatial Query" in a Geographic Information System?
options: Selecting geographic features from one layer based strictly on their spatial relationship (touch, intersect, contain, within distance) to features in another layer
Searching text in a phone directory
Changing the font size of map labels
Calculating the file size on a hard disk
bankQuestions.explanation: A spatial query uses geometric operators (e.g., "Find all school buildings within 500 meters of a major highway") to retrieve features based on location relationships.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Spatial query selects features based on geometric relationships (within distance, contains, touches).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Map Scale" defined as in cartography?
options: The ratio of a distance measured on the map to the corresponding true horizontal distance on the ground
The size of the paper sheet on which the map is printed
The number of colors used in the map legend
The elevation of the highest contour line on the map
bankQuestions.explanation: Map scale expresses the proportional relationship between the representation on the map and the physical distance on the Earth surface: Scale = Map Distance / Ground Distance.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Map Scale = Map Distance / Ground Distance.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which of the following representative fractions represents the largest map scale?
bankQuestions.explanation: A larger scale has a smaller denominator (yielding a larger fraction: 1/500 > 1/250,000). A 1:500 scale shows great detail of a small area, typical of cadastral surveys.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Largest scale = Smallest denominator. 1:500 is a very large scale map.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Indian Geodetic Datum used historically for the Survey of India Topographical Map Sheets?
options: Everest 1830 ellipsoid with origin at Kalianpur (Madhya Pradesh)
WGS 84 ellipsoid with origin at Greenwich
Clarke 1866 ellipsoid with origin at Meades Ranch
GRS 80 ellipsoid with origin at Paris
bankQuestions.explanation: The classical Indian national triangulation system is based on the Everest 1830 reference ellipsoid, with its geodetic datum origin established at Kalianpur.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Survey of India topo sheets historically used the Everest 1830 ellipsoid with Kalianpur datum origin.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the "Almanac" in a GPS receiver?
options: Allowing the receiver to rapidly compute which satellites are visible above the local horizon upon power-up by storing coarse orbital parameters for all satellites
Translating satellite telemetry into regional languages
Calculating tidal rise and fall along the coast
Converting coordinates between WGS84 and local grids
bankQuestions.explanation: The GPS almanac contains approximate orbital data for the entire constellation, enabling the receiver to focus its correlators on visible satellites for fast signal acquisition.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Almanac holds coarse orbital data for all satellites to enable fast initial acquisition.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How many satellites are in each orbital plane of the nominal 24-satellite GPS constellation?
options: 4 satellites per plane across 6 orbital planes
bankQuestions.explanation: The nominal GPS constellation consists of 24 primary satellites evenly distributed with 4 satellites in each of the 6 orbital planes.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Nominal GPS design: 4 satellites in each of 6 orbital planes (24 primary satellites).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In GPS terminology, what does "SA" (Selective Availability) refer to?
options: An intentional degradation of civilian GPS accuracy introduced by the US military, which was permanently discontinued in May 2000
A special antenna for extreme arctic conditions
A feature selecting the strongest satellite automatically
bankQuestions.explanation: Selective Availability (SA) intentionally dithered satellite clock signals and truncated ephemeris to degrade civilian accuracy to ~100m. It was turned off on May 2, 2000.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Selective Availability (SA) was intentional military accuracy degradation, turned off in 2000.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the approximate speed of light (c) in vacuum used in GNSS pseudorange calculations?
bankQuestions.explanation: The exact speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum is standardized as 299,792,458 m/s (~3 x 10^8 m/s).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Speed of light in vacuum c = 299,792,458 m/s.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the purpose of "Station Pointer" in marine cartography?
options: Mechanically solving the Three-Point Problem to fix and plot the sounding station location on nautical charts
Pointing the ship rudder towards the harbour mouth
Measuring water salinity on survey lines
Measuring wave periods from the shore
bankQuestions.explanation: A station pointer is a 3-arm drafting protractor used to plot the position of a sounding boat directly on a chart from two angles observed to three shore stations.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Station pointer mechanically plots the 3-point problem on hydrographic survey sheets.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In AutoCAD, what does WCS stand for?
bankQuestions.explanation: WCS stands for World Coordinate System—the fixed, permanent Cartesian coordinate system that serves as the universal reference frame for all drawings in AutoCAD.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: WCS = World Coordinate System (fixed universal reference frame in AutoCAD).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In AutoCAD, what does UCS stand for?
bankQuestions.explanation: UCS stands for User Coordinate System—a movable, custom coordinate system defined by the draftsman to orient the X, Y, and Z axes to suit specific geometric tasks.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: UCS = User Coordinate System (customizable movable coordinate frame).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the default direction of positive angle measurement in AutoCAD?
bankQuestions.explanation: By mathematical convention, AutoCAD measures positive angles in a counterclockwise direction starting from 0 degrees pointing East along the positive X-axis.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: In AutoCAD, positive angles are measured Counterclockwise starting from 0° East.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which command is used in AutoCAD to specify linear and angular measurement formats, units, and precision?
bankQuestions.explanation: The UNITS command opens the Drawing Units dialog box to set unit types (Decimal, Architectural, Engineering) and angular formats (Decimal Degrees, Deg/Min/Sec, Surveyor units).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: UNITS sets drawing measurement formats, angle styles, and decimal precision.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In AutoCAD, how is a point entered using Absolute Cartesian coordinates?
options: By typing X,Y (e.g., 50,75) measured from the drawing origin (0,0)
By typing @X,Y measured from the last point
By clicking the mouse button only
bankQuestions.explanation: Absolute Cartesian coordinates are entered as X,Y without the @ prefix, locating the point relative to the fixed origin (0,0) of the current coordinate system.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Absolute Cartesian: X,Y (measured from origin 0,0). Relative Cartesian: @X,Y.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In AutoCAD, how is a point entered using Relative Cartesian coordinates?
options: By prefixing with the @ symbol followed by incremental distances: @ΔX,ΔY (e.g., @10,20)
bankQuestions.explanation: The @ symbol denotes relative coordinates, indicating displacement relative to the last picked coordinate point: @deltaX,deltaY.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Relative Cartesian coordinates use the @ symbol: @ΔX,ΔY.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In AutoCAD, how is a point entered using Relative Polar coordinates?
bankQuestions.explanation: Relative polar coordinates specify distance and angle from the last point using the syntax @Distance<Angle.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Relative Polar format: @Distance<Angle (e.g. @50<30).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In AutoCAD, which command defines the outer artificial boundaries for the drawing grid and limits mouse cursor movement when limit checking is enabled?
bankQuestions.explanation: The LIMITS command sets the lower-left and upper-right coordinates of the drawing space; when LIMITS is turned ON, drawing outside these bounds is prevented.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: LIMITS sets lower-left (0,0) and upper-right boundaries of drawing space.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the function of the F1 keyboard shortcut in AutoCAD?
options: Opens the AutoCAD Help documentation window
bankQuestions.explanation: F1 displays the AutoCAD Help system and documentation.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: F1 = Help window.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the function of the F5 keyboard shortcut in AutoCAD when isometric drafting mode is active?
options: Cycles through Isometric planes: Isoplane Top, Isoplane Left, and Isoplane Right
Switches between Model and Paper space
bankQuestions.explanation: When isometric snap is active, F5 (or Ctrl+E) switches the cursor alignment among the three isometric planes: Left (90° and 150°), Top (30° and 150°), and Right (30° and 90°).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: F5 = Cycles Isometric Planes (Top, Left, Right).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the difference between an XLINE and a RAY in AutoCAD?
options: An XLINE extends infinitely in both directions, whereas a RAY starts at a defined root point and extends infinitely in only one direction
An XLINE has finite length while a RAY is infinite
An XLINE creates curved lines while a RAY creates straight lines
A RAY is an optical laser simulation while an XLINE is a drawing line
bankQuestions.explanation: XLINE creates a construction line infinite in both directions. RAY creates a semi-infinite construction line starting from a base point and extending infinitely in a single direction.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: XLINE = infinite in both directions. RAY = infinite in one direction starting from a point.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records
