bankQuestions.rankerTip: Galvanization = coating iron/steel with Zinc for sacrificial corrosion protection.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the chemical composition of "Rust" that forms on iron exposed to moist atmospheric air?
bankQuestions.explanation: Rusting is the electrochemical oxidation of iron in the presence of water and oxygen, producing reddish-brown hydrated ferric oxide: Fe2O3 · xH2O.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Rust = Hydrated Ferric Oxide (Fe2O3 · xH2O). Requires BOTH oxygen and water.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Galvanic Corrosion" (bimetallic corrosion)?
options: Accelerated electrochemical corrosion that occurs when two dissimilar metals are in direct electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte
Corrosion caused by stray lightning strikes
Erosion of copper by sand particles
bankQuestions.explanation: When two different metals touch in an electrolyte, a galvanic cell forms: the less noble (active) metal becomes an anode and corrodes rapidly.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Galvanic corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals contact each other in an electrolyte.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In mechanical belt drives, what is the theoretical velocity ratio (VR) between the driving pulley of diameter D1 (speed N1) and driven pulley of diameter D2 (speed N2), neglecting belt slip and thickness?
bankQuestions.explanation: Assuming no slip, the peripheral linear speed of both pulleys equals belt speed: π D1 N1 = π D2 N2, which yields N2 / N1 = D1 / D2.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Belt velocity ratio: N2 / N1 = D1 / D2 (Speed is inversely proportional to diameter).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: When the thickness "t" of a flat belt is taken into account, what is the corrected velocity ratio of the belt drive?
bankQuestions.explanation: The effective pitch diameter of a pulley is measured to the centerline of the belt: D_eff = D + t. Hence, N2 / N1 = (D1 + t) / (D2 + t).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: With belt thickness t: N2 / N1 = (D1 + t) / (D2 + t).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Creep" in mechanical belt drive operation?
options: The slight relative motion between belt and pulley rim caused by unequal elastic elongation and contraction of the belt between tight and slack sides
The physical slipping of a loose belt under heavy load
The stretching of the belt over months of use
The vibration of the motor mount
bankQuestions.explanation: As the belt passes from the tight side (high tension, stretched) to slack side (low tension, contracted), it contracts over the pulley face. This small elastic motion is creep.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Creep in belts is caused by elastic stretching differences between tight and slack sides.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the formula for the ratio of belt tensions (T1 on tight side, T2 on slack side) for a flat belt drive with coefficient of friction μ and angle of lap θ (in radians)?
bankQuestions.explanation: From differential equilibrium along the belt arc, the limiting ratio of tensions for a flat belt is T1 / T2 = e^(μ θ), where θ is the angle of contact in radians.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Flat belt tension ratio: T1 / T2 = e^(μ θ).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why does a V-belt drive transmit significantly greater power than a flat belt of the same dimensions and tension?
options: Because the wedging action of the V-belt inside the 40-degree grooved pulley creates high normal contact forces, dramatically increasing effective friction
Because V-belts are made of pure steel
bankQuestions.explanation: A V-belt wedges into the pulley groove (groove angle 2β ≈ 34°–40°), boosting effective friction by a factor of 1 / sin(β), providing high grip without slipping.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: V-belt wedging action inside pulley grooves multiplies effective friction and power capacity.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How many revolutions does the crankshaft complete to finish one full thermodynamic cycle in a Four-Stroke Internal Combustion engine?
options: 2 complete revolutions (720 degrees of crankshaft rotation)
bankQuestions.explanation: A four-stroke engine executes 4 piston strokes (Suction, Compression, Power, Exhaust) across 2 complete revolutions of the crankshaft (720°).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: 4-stroke engine = 2 crankshaft revolutions per cycle (1 power stroke per 2 revs).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How many revolutions does the crankshaft complete for each power stroke in a Two-Stroke Internal Combustion engine?
bankQuestions.explanation: In a two-stroke engine, a power stroke occurs during every single revolution of the crankshaft (360°), combining intake/compression and expansion/exhaust.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: 2-stroke engine = 1 crankshaft revolution per power stroke (360°).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the definition of "Compression Ratio" (r) in an internal combustion engine cylinder?
options: The ratio of maximum cylinder volume (Total volume = Swept volume + Clearance volume) to minimum cylinder volume (Clearance volume): r = (Vs + Vc) / Vc
The ratio of power to fuel consumed
The ratio of bore diameter to stroke length
The ratio of intake pressure to exhaust pressure
bankQuestions.explanation: Compression ratio r = Total Cylinder Volume / Clearance Volume = (Vs + Vc) / Vc, where Vs is swept volume and Vc is clearance volume.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Compression ratio r = (Swept Volume + Clearance Volume) / Clearance Volume.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the typical compression ratio range for standard four-stroke Petrol (Spark Ignition - SI) engines?
bankQuestions.explanation: Petrol engines operate with compression ratios between 6:1 and 10:1 to avoid auto-ignition (engine knocking/detonation) of the petrol-air mixture before the spark fires.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Petrol (SI) engine compression ratio = 6:1 to 10:1. Diesel (CI) engine = 14:1 to 22:1.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the typical compression ratio range for standard Diesel (Compression Ignition - CI) engines?
bankQuestions.explanation: Diesel engines rely on high compression heat to ignite injected fuel, requiring compression ratios between 14:1 and 22:1.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Diesel engine compression ratio = 14:1 to 22:1 (high enough to auto-ignite injected diesel).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is Euler Formula relating the number of Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F) for any convex polyhedron?
bankQuestions.explanation: Euler Polyhedral Formula states that for every convex polyhedron: Vertices - Edges + Faces = 2 (e.g. for a cube: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Euler Polyhedral Formula: V - E + F = 2.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How many total Faces, Edges, and Vertices does a regular Tetrahedron have?
bankQuestions.explanation: A regular tetrahedron has 4 equilateral triangular faces, 6 edges, and 4 vertices (4 - 6 + 4 = 2).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Tetrahedron: 4 faces, 6 edges, 4 vertices.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the Prismoidal Formula (Simpson Rule for volumes), what is the volume V of an earthwork prismoid of length L with end areas A1, A2 and mid-area Am?
bankQuestions.explanation: The Prismoidal formula computes exact volume: V = (L / 6) * (A1 + 4Am + A2), where Am is the area calculated from mid-dimensions.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Prismoidal Volume = (L / 6) x (A1 + 4Am + A2).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the Trapezoidal Rule (Average End Area method), what is the volume V of an excavation cut between two cross-sections of areas A1 and A2 separated by distance L?
bankQuestions.explanation: The average end area formula averages the two ends: V = [(A1 + A2) / 2] * L = (L / 2) * (A1 + A2).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Average End Area volume V = (L / 2) x (A1 + A2).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Prismoidal Correction" (Cp) subtracted from the average end area earthwork volume to obtain the true prismoidal volume?
options: Cp = (L / 6) * (h1 - h2) * (w1 - w2) for rectangular cuts, meaning average end area method always overestimates volume
Prismoidal correction is zero for all shapes
bankQuestions.explanation: The Average End Area method mathematically overestimates earthwork volumes for convex ground shapes. The prismoidal correction is always positive and must be subtracted.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Average End Area method overestimates volume; Prismoidal correction is subtracted.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the formula for the distance d between two coordinate points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) in a plane Cartesian system?
bankQuestions.explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem in a coordinate plane: Distance d = √[(x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2].
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Distance formula: d = √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²].
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the section formula, what are the coordinates of the point dividing the line segment between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) internally in the ratio m : n?
bankQuestions.explanation: Internal section formula: x = (m x2 + n x1) / (m + n) and y = (m y2 + n y1) / (m + n).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Internal division: [(m x2 + n x1)/(m + n), (m y2 + n y1)/(m + n)].
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What are the coordinates of the Centroid of a triangle with vertices at (x1, y1), (x2, y2), and (x3, y3)?
bankQuestions.explanation: The centroid coordinates are the arithmetic averages of the vertex coordinates: G = [(x1 + x2 + x3)/3, (y1 + y2 + y3)/3].
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Triangle Centroid: x_c = (x1 + x2 + x3)/3, y_c = (y1 + y2 + y3)/3.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the condition for two straight lines with slopes m1 and m2 to be strictly perpendicular to each other?
bankQuestions.explanation: Two lines are perpendicular if their slopes satisfy m1 * m2 = -1 (the slope of one is the negative reciprocal of the other: m2 = -1 / m1).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Perpendicular lines: m1 x m2 = -1. Parallel lines: m1 = m2.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the perpendicular distance (d) from a point (x1, y1) to the straight line given by the general equation Ax + By + C = 0?
bankQuestions.explanation: The formula for perpendicular distance from point to line is d = |A x1 + B y1 + C| / √(A^2 + B^2).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Distance from point to line: d = |Ax1 + By1 + C| / √(A² + B²).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In geometry, what is the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference of a circle (angle in a semicircle)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Thales Theorem states that the angle inscribed in a semicircle is always a right angle (90°).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Angle in a semicircle = 90° (right angle).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In circle geometry, what is the sum of the opposite interior angles of any cyclic quadrilateral?
bankQuestions.explanation: For any quadrilateral inscribed in a circle (cyclic quadrilateral), the sum of opposite angles is always 180° (A + C = 180° and B + D = 180°).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles sum to 180°.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the Intersecting Chords Theorem, if two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at an internal point P, what relation holds true?
bankQuestions.explanation: By similar triangles, when two chords AB and CD intersect inside a circle at point P: PA * PB = PC * PD.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Intersecting chords: PA x PB = PC x PD.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the Tangent-Secant Theorem, if a secant PAB and a tangent PT are drawn to a circle from an external point P, what relation holds true?
bankQuestions.explanation: The tangent-secant theorem states that the square of the tangent segment from an external point equals the product of the external secant segment and entire secant: PT^2 = PA * PB.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Tangent-Secant Theorem: PT² = PA x PB.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Velocity Ratio (VR) of the First System of Pulleys consisting of "n" movable pulleys suspended by separate ropes attached to an overhead beam?
bankQuestions.explanation: In the first system of pulleys, each additional movable pulley doubles the velocity ratio: VR = 2^n, where n is the number of movable pulleys.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: First system of pulleys: VR = 2^n.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Velocity Ratio (VR) of the Second System of Pulleys (Block and Tackle) having a total of "n" pulleys distributed between the fixed and movable blocks?
options: VR = n (the total number of pulleys in both blocks)
bankQuestions.explanation: In a standard block and tackle with a single continuous rope, the velocity ratio equals the total number of pulleys (n) in both top and bottom blocks combined: VR = n.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Second system of pulleys (block & tackle): VR = n (total number of pulleys).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Velocity Ratio (VR) of the Third System of Pulleys comprising "n" total pulleys where all strings are attached to the load block?
bankQuestions.explanation: In the third system of pulleys, the total velocity ratio is the sum of a geometric series: VR = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(n-1) = 2^n - 1.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Third system of pulleys: VR = 2^n - 1.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Velocity Ratio (VR) of a Weston Differential Pulley Block having a large pulley diameter D and small stepped pulley diameter d?
bankQuestions.explanation: In one revolution of the compound upper block, the effort moves π D while the load rises (π D - π d)/2: VR = π D / [(π D - π d)/2] = 2D / (D - d).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Weston differential pulley: VR = 2D / (D - d).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Velocity Ratio (VR) of a Worm and Worm Wheel machine having a single-start worm and a worm wheel with T teeth, operated by an effort wheel of radius R and load drum of radius r?
bankQuestions.explanation: One rotation of the effort wheel turns the worm once, advancing the worm wheel by 1 tooth (1/T rev). The load moves 2πr / T while effort moves 2πR: VR = (R * T) / r.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Worm and worm wheel VR = (R x T) / r.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Curie Temperature" of a ferromagnetic material such as iron?
options: The critical temperature above which the material completely loses its permanent ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic (770 °C for iron)
The melting point of the metal
The boiling point of liquid nitrogen
The temperature at which electrical resistance becomes zero
bankQuestions.explanation: Above the Curie temperature (770°C for iron), thermal agitation destroys the parallel alignment of magnetic domains, turning the ferromagnetic material into a paramagnetic state.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Curie Temperature = critical temperature where ferromagnetism transitions to paramagnetism (770°C for iron).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What magnetic property characterizes "Diamagnetic" materials (such as bismuth, copper, and water)?
options: They have relative magnetic permeability slightly less than 1 (μr < 1) and are weakly repelled by a magnetic field
They are strongly attracted by magnets
bankQuestions.explanation: Diamagnetic substances (bismuth, copper, gold, water) have μr slightly less than 1 and negative susceptibility; they are feebly repelled by magnetic poles.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Diamagnetic: μr < 1, feebly repelled by magnets (copper, bismuth, water).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What magnetic property characterizes "Paramagnetic" materials (such as aluminum and platinum)?
options: They have relative magnetic permeability slightly greater than 1 (μr > 1) and are weakly attracted by a magnetic field
They are strongly repelled by magnetic poles
bankQuestions.explanation: Paramagnetic substances (aluminum, platinum, manganese) have relative permeability slightly greater than 1 (μr > 1); they are feebly attracted by magnets in direction of increasing field.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Paramagnetic: μr slightly > 1, feebly attracted by magnets (aluminum, platinum).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why is Soft Iron preferred over steel as the magnetic core material in electromagnets and transformer cores?
options: Because soft iron has high magnetic permeability, low coercivity, and narrow hysteresis loss, magnetizing and demagnetizing instantly
Because soft iron is harder than steel
Because soft iron never conducts electricity
bankQuestions.explanation: Soft iron exhibits high magnetic permeability and small retentivity/coercivity. It magnetizes readily when current flows and demagnetizes immediately when current is cut off.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Electromagnets use soft iron: high permeability, low retentivity and coercivity.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why is Alnico (or high-carbon tungsten steel) preferred for making Permanent Magnets?
options: Because it possesses high magnetic retentivity and high coercivity, resisting demagnetization by stray fields
Because it melts at low temperature
Because it is cheap to cast
bankQuestions.explanation: Permanent magnets require materials with large hysteresis loops, high retentivity (strong remaining magnetism), and high coercivity (resistance to being demagnetized).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Permanent magnets require high retentivity and high coercivity (e.g. Alnico).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How is a sensitive moving-coil Galvanometer converted into an Ammeter capable of measuring large electrical currents?
options: By connecting a low-resistance resistor (Shunt) in parallel across the galvanometer coil
By connecting a high-resistance resistor in series
By winding the coil with aluminum wire
bankQuestions.explanation: A shunt is a very low resistance connected in parallel with the galvanometer. Most current bypasses the delicate meter coil through the shunt, enabling high current measurement.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Galvanometer to Ammeter = LOW resistance (Shunt) in PARALLEL.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How is a moving-coil Galvanometer converted into a Voltmeter capable of measuring high electrical voltages?
options: By connecting a high-resistance multiplier resistor in series with the galvanometer coil
By connecting a low resistance in parallel
By immersing the coil in oil
bankQuestions.explanation: Connecting a large resistance in series with the galvanometer coil limits current flow to safe microamperes when placed across large potential differences.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Galvanometer to Voltmeter = HIGH resistance in SERIES.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What fundamental conservation law forms the physical basis of Kirchhoff Current Law (KCL)?
options: Law of Conservation of Electric Charge
Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum
bankQuestions.explanation: KCL states that charge cannot accumulate at an electrical node: total current entering equals total current leaving (ΣI = 0), based on conservation of charge.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Kirchhoff Current Law (KCL) is based on Conservation of Charge (ΣI = 0).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What fundamental conservation law forms the physical basis of Kirchhoff Voltage Law (KVL)?
options: Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
bankQuestions.explanation: KVL states that the sum of potential gains and drops around any closed electrical loop is zero (ΣV = 0), which is a direct statement of conservation of energy.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Kirchhoff Voltage Law (KVL) is based on Conservation of Energy (ΣV = 0).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the condition for balance in a Wheatstone Bridge circuit with four resistance arms P, Q, R, and S?
options: P / Q = R / S (no current flows through the central galvanometer)
bankQuestions.explanation: When the potential at opposite bridge terminals is equal, no current flows through the galvanometer. The balance condition is P / Q = R / S.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Wheatstone Bridge balance condition: P / Q = R / S.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Eccentricity (e) of a Parabola in conic sections?
bankQuestions.explanation: A parabola is defined as the locus of a point whose distance from the focus equals its distance from the directrix; hence eccentricity e = 1.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Eccentricity values: Circle e = 0, Ellipse e < 1, Parabola e = 1, Hyperbola e > 1.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Eccentricity (e) of an Ellipse in conic sections?
options: e is strictly less than 1 (0 < e < 1)
bankQuestions.explanation: An ellipse is the locus of a point whose distance from the focus is less than its distance from the directrix (e < 1).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Ellipse eccentricity: 0 < e < 1.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Eccentricity (e) of a Hyperbola in conic sections?
bankQuestions.explanation: A hyperbola is the locus of a point whose distance from the focus exceeds its distance from the directrix (e > 1).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Hyperbola eccentricity: e > 1. Rectangular hyperbola: e = √2.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Eccentricity (e) of a perfect Circle in conic sections?
bankQuestions.explanation: A circle is a special case of an ellipse whose two foci merge into a single center point, giving eccentricity e = 0.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Circle eccentricity: e = 0.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the length of the Latus Rectum of a standard parabola y^2 = 4ax?
bankQuestions.explanation: The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the axis of symmetry. For y^2 = 4ax, x = a gives y^2 = 4a^2, y = ±2a, so length = 4a.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Parabola y² = 4ax latus rectum length = 4a.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the length of the Latus Rectum of an ellipse with semi-major axis "a" and semi-minor axis "b"?
bankQuestions.explanation: For ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1, setting x = ae gives y = ±b^2/a, yielding total latus rectum length = 2b^2 / a.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Ellipse latus rectum length = 2b² / a.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the center and radius of a circle represented by the general equation x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0?
options: Center = (g, f) and Radius = √(g^2 + f^2 + c)
Center = (-g, -f) and Radius = g + f - c
bankQuestions.explanation: Completing the square gives (x + g)^2 + (y + f)^2 = g^2 + f^2 - c, so center is (-g, -f) and radius is √(g^2 + f^2 - c).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: General circle equation: Center = (-g, -f), Radius = √(g² + f² - c).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Anomalous Expansion of Water" between 0 °C and 4 °C?
options: Water contracts as it is heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, reaching its maximum density and minimum volume at exactly 4 °C
Water expands uniformly at all temperatures
bankQuestions.explanation: Unlike other liquids, water contracts when warmed from 0°C to 4°C due to collapsing hydrogen bonds, achieving its peak density of 1000 kg/m³ at 4°C.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Water reaches MAXIMUM density and MINIMUM volume at 4 °C (1000 kg/m³).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why do aquatic creatures survive at the bottom of frozen lakes during severe winter climates?
options: Because water reaches maximum density at 4 °C and sinks to the bottom, while lighter ice (density ~917 kg/m³) floats on top acting as an insulating blanket
Because the lake bed has thermal vents
bankQuestions.explanation: Water at 4°C is denser than water at 0°C or ice. The dense 4°C water remains at the lake bed, while ice stays on the surface, keeping bottom waters liquid.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Water 4°C maximum density keeps lake bottoms liquid under insulating surface ice.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Triple Point of Water"?
options: The unique state of thermodynamic equilibrium at 0.01 °C (273.16 K) and 611.65 Pa where solid ice, liquid water, and water vapor coexist simultaneously
The temperature at which water boils
The critical point of steam turbines
The point where water turns to ice at 0 °C
bankQuestions.explanation: At the triple point (273.16 K / 0.01°C and 4.58 mmHg / 611.65 Pa), all three phases of water exist in stable equilibrium, serving as the international definition for the Kelvin scale.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Triple point of water = 273.16 K (0.01 °C) and 611.65 Pa (ice, water, and steam coexist).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which law of thermodynamics establishes the concept of Temperature and thermal equilibrium between systems?
bankQuestions.explanation: The Zeroth Law states that if bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with body C, they are in equilibrium with each other, defining temperature as a measurable property.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Zeroth Law defines Temperature. First Law = Energy Conservation. Second Law = Entropy.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does the First Law of Thermodynamics state mathematically for a closed system undergoing a change of state?
options: ΔQ = ΔU + W (Heat added = Increase in internal energy + Work done by system)
bankQuestions.explanation: The First Law expresses conservation of energy: ΔQ = ΔU + W, where ΔQ is heat supplied, ΔU is internal energy change, and W is work performed.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: 1st Law of Thermodynamics: ΔQ = ΔU + W (Conservation of Energy).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics dictate regarding spontaneous heat transfer?
options: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body without an external supply of work (Clausius statement)
Heat always flows from cold to hot
Perpetual motion machines of the second kind are 100% possible
Total entropy of the universe decreases
bankQuestions.explanation: The Clausius statement of the 2nd Law states that heat cannot flow unaided from a low-temperature reservoir to a high-temperature reservoir without work input (refrigeration).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: 2nd Law: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from cold to hot without external work.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the magnetic circuit analogue of electrical resistance (the opposition offered to magnetic flux)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Reluctance is the resistance offered by a magnetic circuit to the passage of magnetic flux lines: R_m = l / (μ * A). Its unit is Ampere-turns per Weber (AT/Wb) or H^-1.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Magnetic Reluctance = opposition to magnetic flux (analogue of electrical resistance).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the SI unit of Magnetomotive Force (MMF)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Magnetomotive force is the magnetic potential driving flux through a circuit: MMF = N * I, measured in Ampere-turns (AT).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: MMF unit = Ampere-turns (AT). Magnetic Flux = Weber (Wb).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the formula for the electrical energy (E in Joules) stored in an inductor of inductance L carrying current I?
bankQuestions.explanation: The magnetic energy stored in an inductor coil is E = (1/2) * L * I^2 Joules.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Inductor stored energy: E = (1/2) L I² Joules.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the formula for the electrical energy (E in Joules) stored in a capacitor of capacitance C charged to voltage V?
bankQuestions.explanation: The electrostatic energy stored in a charged capacitor is E = (1/2) C V^2 = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) Q^2 / C.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Capacitor stored energy: E = (1/2) C V² = (1/2) Q V.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the SI unit of Electrical Inductance (self or mutual inductance)?
bankQuestions.explanation: The Henry (H) is the SI unit of inductance, defined as 1 Volt of induced EMF when current changes at 1 Ampere per second (1 H = 1 V·s/A).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Inductance unit = Henry (H). Capacitance = Farad (F).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to Brahmagupta Formula, what is the area of a cyclic quadrilateral having side lengths a, b, c, and d?
options: Area = √[(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)] where s = (a + b + c + d) / 2
bankQuestions.explanation: Brahmagupta Formula gives the area of a cyclic quadrilateral: Area = √[(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)], where s is semi-perimeter.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Brahmagupta Formula: Area of cyclic quadrilateral = √[(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)].
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to Ptolemy Theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals, what does the product of the two diagonals equal?
options: The sum of the products of opposite pairs of sides: d1 * d2 = a * c + b * d
The product of all four sides
The sum of all four sides squared
bankQuestions.explanation: Ptolemy Theorem states that in a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides: AC * BD = AB * CD + BC * DA.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Ptolemy Theorem: d1 x d2 = ac + bd.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the mathematical formula for the number of internal diagonals in an n-sided polygon?
bankQuestions.explanation: From combinatorics, choosing 2 vertices from n gives n(n-1)/2 lines. Subtracting the n outer perimeter sides leaves n(n-1)/2 - n = n(n-3)/2 diagonals.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Polygon diagonals = n(n - 3) / 2. (Hexagon = 9, Octagon = 20).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the sum of all exterior angles for ANY convex polygon, regardless of the number of sides?
bankQuestions.explanation: The sum of the exterior angles of any closed convex polygon is always equal to 360° (or 4 right angles), as a complete turn around the perimeter returns to the start direction.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sum of exterior angles of ANY convex polygon = 360°.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Why does the Center of Pressure on a submerged vertical planar surface always lie strictly below the Centroid (Center of Gravity) of the surface?
options: Because hydrostatic fluid pressure increases linearly with depth, exerting greater force on the lower portions of the surface
Because atmospheric pressure acts at the top
bankQuestions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh grows with depth, so the centroid of the pressure distribution prism lies lower than the geometric centroid of the submerged area: h* = h_bar + Ig/(A*h_bar).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Center of pressure is always BELOW the centroid because pressure increases with depth.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Where is the Center of Pressure located for a vertical rectangular plane of depth "d" having its upper edge lying in the free liquid surface?
options: At a depth of (2 / 3) * d from the liquid surface
bankQuestions.explanation: For a vertical rectangle with top at surface, centroid is at d/2 and moment of inertia is bd^3/12: h* = d/2 + (bd^3/12)/(bd * d/2) = d/2 + d/6 = 2d/3.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Center of pressure for vertical rectangle with top at surface = (2/3) d.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Where is the Center of Pressure located for a vertical triangular plane of height "h" having its base in the free liquid surface and vertex pointing downward?
options: At a depth of h / 2 from the free liquid surface
bankQuestions.explanation: For a triangle with base at surface, centroid is h/3 below surface: h* = h/3 + (b h^3 / 36) / [(0.5 b h) * (h/3)] = h/3 + h/6 = h/2.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Vertical triangle with base at surface: Center of pressure = h / 2.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Where is the Center of Pressure located for a vertical triangular plane of height "h" having its vertex in the liquid surface and base horizontal at depth h?
options: At a depth of (3 / 4) * h from the free liquid surface
bankQuestions.explanation: With vertex at surface, centroid is at 2h/3: h* = 2h/3 + (b h^3 / 36) / [(0.5 b h) * (2h/3)] = 2h/3 + h/12 = 3h/4.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Vertical triangle with vertex at surface: Center of pressure = (3/4) h.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the classic Flexure Formula (Bending Equation) for pure bending of beams within the elastic limit?
options: M / I = σ / y = E / R
M * I = σ * y = E * R
M / y = σ / I = R / E
M / E = I / σ = y / R
bankQuestions.explanation: The Euler-Bernoulli beam bending equation is M / I = σ / y = E / R, relating bending moment M, moment of inertia I, bending stress σ, fiber distance y, Young modulus E, and radius of curvature R.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Beam Bending Equation: M / I = σ / y = E / R.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Section Modulus (Z) of a structural beam defined as?
options: The ratio of the moment of inertia (I) about the neutral axis to the distance (ymax) of the extreme outer fiber: Z = I / ymax
The product of area and length
The shear stress divided by strain
The bending moment divided by span
bankQuestions.explanation: Section Modulus Z = I / ymax. It measures beam flexural strength against bending: maximum resisting moment M_R = σ_allowable * Z.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Section Modulus Z = I / ymax. Bending strength M = σ Z.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Section Modulus (Z) of a solid rectangular beam cross-section of width "b" and depth "d"?
bankQuestions.explanation: For a rectangle, I = b d^3 / 12 and ymax = d / 2. Therefore, Z = (b d^3 / 12) / (d / 2) = b d^2 / 6.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Rectangular section modulus Z = (b d²) / 6. Moment of inertia I = (b d³) / 12.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Section Modulus (Z) of a solid circular cross-section of diameter "d"?
bankQuestions.explanation: For a solid circle, I = π d^4 / 64 and ymax = d / 2. Thus Z = (π d^4 / 64) / (d / 2) = π d^3 / 32.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Solid circular Section Modulus Z = (π d³) / 32. Polar section modulus Zp = (π d³) / 16.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Moment of Inertia (I) of a solid rectangular cross-section of width b and depth d about its centroidal horizontal axis?
bankQuestions.explanation: The second moment of area (moment of inertia) of a rectangle about its neutral horizontal centroidal axis is I_x = b d^3 / 12.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Rectangular centroidal Moment of Inertia I = (b d³) / 12. About base: I_base = (b d³) / 3.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Moment of Inertia (I) of a solid circular area of diameter "d" about any diameter axis passing through its center?
bankQuestions.explanation: The diametral moment of inertia of a circular area is I = π d^4 / 64 = π r^4 / 4.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Circular Moment of Inertia I = (π d⁴) / 64. Polar moment of inertia J = (π d⁴) / 32.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Law of Machine" relating applied effort (P) to lifted load (W)?
options: P = m * W + C (where m is slope constant and C is effort required to overcome zero-load machine friction)
bankQuestions.explanation: The empirical straight-line equation relating effort and load is P = mW + C, where m represents friction increasing with load and C is idle friction.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Law of Machine: P = m W + C.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the Law of Machine (P = mW + C), what is the theoretical Maximum Mechanical Advantage (MA_max) obtainable by the machine as load W becomes very large?
bankQuestions.explanation: Since MA = W / P = W / (mW + C) = 1 / [m + (C/W)], as W approaches infinity, C/W becomes 0, yielding MA_max = 1 / m.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Maximum Mechanical Advantage MA_max = 1 / m.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to the Law of Machine, what is the theoretical Maximum Efficiency (η_max) of the machine?
bankQuestions.explanation: Maximum efficiency η_max = MA_max / VR = (1 / m) / VR = 1 / (m * VR).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Maximum machine efficiency: η_max = 1 / (m x VR).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: When is a lifting screw mechanism classified as "Overhauling"?
options: When the helix angle of the thread exceeds the friction angle (α > ϕ), causing the load to drop or unscrew on its own when effort is removed
When the screw is jammed by grit
bankQuestions.explanation: An overhauling screw reverses automatically under load because the helix angle exceeds the angle of friction (α > ϕ, efficiency > 50%).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Overhauling occurs when helix angle α > friction angle ϕ (machine reverses under load).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Parallel Axis Theorem (Steiner Theorem) for the area Moment of Inertia of a plane lamina?
options: I_axis = I_G + A * d^2 (where I_G is centroidal moment of inertia, A is area, and d is distance between parallel axes)
bankQuestions.explanation: The parallel axis theorem states: I_axis = I_G + A * d^2, where I_G is the moment of inertia about the parallel centroidal axis and d is axis separation.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Parallel Axis Theorem: I_parallel = I_G + A d².
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Perpendicular Axis Theorem for the area Moment of Inertia of a thin plane lamina lying in the X-Y plane?
options: I_z = I_x + I_y (the polar moment of inertia equals the sum of moments of inertia about two mutually perpendicular in-plane axes)
bankQuestions.explanation: For a flat 2D lamina in the X-Y plane, the perpendicular axis theorem establishes that I_z = I_x + I_y.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Perpendicular Axis Theorem: I_z = I_x + I_y.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the definition of the "Radius of Gyration" (k) of a plane area having area A and moment of inertia I?
options: k = √(I / A), so that I = A * k^2
bankQuestions.explanation: The radius of gyration k is the distance from the reference axis at which the entire area could be concentrated without altering its moment of inertia: k = √(I / A).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Radius of gyration k = √(I / A), giving I = A k².
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Moment of Inertia (I) of a triangular cross-section of base "b" and height "h" about its base edge?
bankQuestions.explanation: The moment of inertia of a triangle about its base is I_base = b h^3 / 12. (About its centroidal axis parallel to base it is I_G = b h^3 / 36).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Triangle Moment of Inertia: About base = (b h³) / 12. About centroid = (b h³) / 36.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Moment of Inertia (I_G) of a triangular cross-section of base "b" and height "h" about its centroidal axis parallel to the base?
bankQuestions.explanation: By parallel axis theorem: I_G = I_base - A * d^2 = (b h^3 / 12) - (0.5 b h) * (h / 3)^2 = b h^3 / 12 - b h^3 / 18 = b h^3 / 36.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Triangle centroidal Moment of Inertia I_G = (b h³) / 36.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the standard Torsion Formula for circular solid or hollow shafts subjected to twisting torque T within the elastic limit?
options: T / J = τ / r = (G * θ) / L
T * J = τ * r = G * θ
T / r = τ / J = L / (G * θ)
T / L = τ / G = J / θ
bankQuestions.explanation: The torsion formula for circular shafts is T / J = τ / r = (G * θ) / L, where J is polar moment of inertia, τ is shear stress at radius r, G is shear modulus, and θ is angle of twist.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Torsion Formula: T / J = τ / r = (G θ) / L.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Polar Section Modulus (Z_p) of a solid circular shaft of diameter "d"?
bankQuestions.explanation: Polar section modulus Z_p = J / r = (π d^4 / 32) / (d / 2) = π d^3 / 16. It determines the torsional shear carrying capacity T = τ * Z_p.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Solid circular Polar Section Modulus Z_p = (π d³) / 16.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Torsional Rigidity" of a circular transmission shaft defined as?
options: The product of Modulus of Rigidity (G) and Polar Moment of Inertia (J): G * J
The shear stress divided by angle of twist
bankQuestions.explanation: Torsional rigidity is the torque required to produce unit angle of twist per unit shaft length: Torsional Rigidity = G * J.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Torsional Rigidity = G x J. Torsional Stiffness = (G x J) / L.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How does the stress produced in a bar by a Suddenly Applied Load (without shock) compare to the stress produced if the exact same load is applied gradually?
options: The suddenly applied stress is exactly TWICE the gradually applied stress (σ_sudden = 2 * σ_gradual)
The suddenly applied stress is half
The suddenly applied stress is four times larger
bankQuestions.explanation: Equating work done by falling load P*δ to strain energy (0.5 * σ * δ * Volume) shows that instantaneous stress for a sudden load is exactly 2P/A = 2 * σ_gradual.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Suddenly applied load produces TWICE the stress of a gradually applied load (σ_sudden = 2 σ_gradual).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What are "Principal Planes" in the analysis of two-dimensional complex stress states?
options: Planes on which the shear stress is strictly ZERO (τ = 0), carrying only pure normal tensile or compressive stresses
Planes inclined at 45 degrees to the principal axes
Planes where normal stress is zero
Planes along which failure always occurs
bankQuestions.explanation: Principal planes are defined as the mutually perpendicular planes along which shear stress vanishes completely (τ = 0). The normal stresses on these planes are Principal Stresses.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Principal planes carry ZERO shear stress (τ = 0); normal stresses on them are Principal Stresses.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: In Mohr Circle of Stress for plane stress, what does the Radius of the circle represent?
options: The Maximum Shear Stress (τ_max) acting in the material
bankQuestions.explanation: The radius of Mohr stress circle is R = √[((σx - σy)/2)^2 + τxy^2], which equals the maximum in-plane shear stress τ_max.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Mohr Circle radius = Maximum Shear Stress τ_max.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the coordinates of the Center of Mohr Circle of Stress for a state of plane stress with normal stresses σx and σy?
bankQuestions.explanation: The center of Mohr circle lies on the normal stress (horizontal) axis at the average normal stress: Center = [ (σx + σy) / 2, 0 ].
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Mohr Circle center = [ (σx + σy) / 2, 0 ] on the horizontal axis.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Proof Resilience" in engineering mechanics of materials?
options: The maximum strain energy that can be stored in a body up to the elastic limit without undergoing permanent deformation
The energy needed to melt the metal
bankQuestions.explanation: Resilience is strain energy capacity. Proof resilience is the maximum elastic strain energy absorbed up to the elastic limit: U_proof = (σ_elastic^2 / 2E) * Volume.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Proof Resilience = maximum strain energy stored within the elastic limit.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the "Modulus of Resilience" of a material defined as?
options: The proof resilience per unit volume of the material: (σ_e^2) / (2 * E)
The proof resilience multiplied by volume
The Young modulus divided by shear modulus
bankQuestions.explanation: Modulus of resilience is proof resilience per unit volume, equal to σ_e^2 / (2E), representing the area under the elastic portion of the stress-strain curve.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Modulus of Resilience = Proof Resilience per unit volume = σ_e² / (2E).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: On which planes does the Maximum Shear Stress act relative to the Principal Planes in a 2D stress system?
options: On planes inclined at 45 degrees to the principal planes
On planes parallel to the principal planes
On planes at 90 degrees to the principal planes
On planes at 30 degrees to the principal planes
bankQuestions.explanation: The planes of maximum shear stress are oriented at 45° to the principal planes, and the magnitude of maximum shear stress is half the difference of principal stresses: (σ1 - σ2) / 2.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Maximum shear stress occurs on planes inclined at 45° to the principal planes.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Volume (V) of a triangular prism of length L having a triangular cross-sectional base of width b and altitude h?
bankQuestions.explanation: Volume of any right prism is Base Area x Length. Here, Base Area = (1/2) * b * h, so Volume V = (1/2) * b * h * L.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Triangular prism Volume = 0.5 x b x h x L.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Volume of a regular square pyramid with base side length "a" and vertical height "h"?
bankQuestions.explanation: Volume of a right pyramid = (1/3) * Base Area * Height = (1/3) * a^2 * h.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Square pyramid Volume = (1/3) a² h.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the formula for the volume of a Frustum of a regular pyramid with height h and end base areas A1 and A2?
bankQuestions.explanation: The volume of a pyramidal frustum is V = (h / 3) * [A1 + A2 + √(A1 * A2)].
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Pyramid frustum Volume = (h / 3) x [A1 + A2 + √(A1 A2)].
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the sum of the interior angles of a regular 10-sided polygon (Decagon)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) * 180°. For n = 10: (10 - 2) * 180° = 8 * 180° = 1,440°. Each interior angle = 1440° / 10 = 144°.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Decagon: Sum of interior angles = 1440°, each interior angle = 144°.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the sum of the interior angles of a regular 5-sided polygon (Pentagon)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Sum of interior angles = (5 - 2) * 180° = 3 * 180° = 540°. Each interior angle = 540° / 5 = 108°.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Pentagon: Sum of interior angles = 540°, each interior angle = 108°.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under geological classification, how are rocks formed by the cooling and solidification of molten magma categorized?
bankQuestions.explanation: Igneous rocks (e.g. granite, basalt, trap) originate from the cooling and crystallization of molten rock magma beneath or on the Earth surface.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Igneous = solidified from molten magma (Granite, Basalt, Trap).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under geological classification, what type of igneous rock is Granite, which cools slowly at great depth beneath the Earth surface?
bankQuestions.explanation: Granite is a plutonic intrusive igneous rock formed by the extremely slow cooling of magma deep underground, giving it a coarse crystalline texture.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Granite is a deep-seated Plutonic intrusive igneous rock.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under geological classification, what type of igneous rock is Basalt, which solidifies rapidly on the Earth surface from volcanic lava?
bankQuestions.explanation: Basalt is an extrusive volcanic igneous rock formed by the rapid cooling of lava exposed on the Earth surface, giving it a fine-grained, dense texture.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Basalt and Trap are Volcanic extrusive igneous rocks.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under geological classification, how are Sandstone and Limestone categorized based on their rock formation process?
bankQuestions.explanation: Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary rocks formed by the gradual deposition, compaction, and cementation of mineral particles and sediment layers.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sandstone, Limestone, Shale, and Conglomerate are Sedimentary rocks.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which metamorphic rock is formed by the metamorphism of pure sedimentary Limestone under high geological heat and pressure?
bankQuestions.explanation: When limestone (calcite CaCO3) undergoes thermal metamorphism, it recrystallizes into crystalline Marble.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Limestone metamorphoses into Marble. Sandstone into Quartzite. Granite into Gneiss.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which metamorphic rock is formed by the metamorphism of sedimentary Sandstone?
bankQuestions.explanation: Quartzite is formed when quartz-rich sedimentary sandstone undergoes intense thermal and pressure metamorphism.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Sandstone metamorphoses into Quartzite (hard, weather-resistant siliceous rock).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which metamorphic rock is formed by the regional dynamic metamorphism of sedimentary Shale or clay?
bankQuestions.explanation: Slate is an argillaceous metamorphic rock formed by the low-grade regional metamorphism of shale and clay, characterized by slaty cleavage.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Shale metamorphoses into Slate.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which metamorphic rock is formed by the metamorphism of deep-seated igneous Granite?
bankQuestions.explanation: Under intense regional metamorphism, granite transforms into foliated, banded Gneiss.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Granite metamorphoses into Gneiss.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under physical classification, rocks that exhibit distinct bedding planes and split easily into parallel layers are called:
bankQuestions.explanation: Stratified rocks (such as sandstone, limestone, and shale) possess layered sedimentary bedding planes along which they split readily.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Stratified rocks have layered bedding planes (sedimentary rocks).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under physical classification, rocks that possess a massive crystalline structure with no layered bedding planes are called:
bankQuestions.explanation: Unstratified rocks (such as granite, basalt, and trap) have monolithic crystalline structures without distinct natural cleavage layers.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Unstratified rocks have no layering (igneous rocks like Granite and Basalt).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under chemical classification of rocks, which group is characterized by Silica (SiO2) as the predominant chemical constituent?
bankQuestions.explanation: Siliceous rocks (granite, quartzite, sandstone, gneiss) contain silica as their main constituent; they are hard, durable, and highly weather-resistant.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Siliceous rocks: Silica predominates (Granite, Quartzite, Sandstone).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under chemical classification, which group of rocks has Alumina or clay as its principal constituent (such as slate and laterite)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Argillaceous rocks (slate, clay, shale, laterite) are composed primarily of alumina (Al2O3) and clay minerals.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Argillaceous rocks: Alumina/clay predominates (Slate, Laterite, Shale).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Under chemical classification, which group of rocks has Calcium Carbonate (lime, CaCO3) as its predominant constituent?
bankQuestions.explanation: Calcareous rocks (limestone, marble, dolomite) contain calcium carbonate as their major constituent.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Calcareous rocks: Calcium carbonate (lime) predominates (Limestone, Marble).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the minimum crushing (compressive) strength required for a stone to be considered acceptable as good building stone?
bankQuestions.explanation: A good building stone should have a minimum compressive crushing strength of at least 100 N/mm² (1000 kg/cm² or 100 MPa).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Good building stone minimum compressive strength = 100 N/mm² (1000 kg/cm²).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the maximum percentage of water absorption by dry weight permitted for a stone to be classified as suitable for building construction?
options: 5% of dry weight (stones absorbing more than 10% are strictly rejected)
bankQuestions.explanation: Good building stones should absorb less than 5% water by weight after 24 hours of immersion. Stones absorbing over 10% are rejected as porous.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Building stone water absorption: should be < 5%; rejected if > 10%.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the typical specific gravity of a good building stone used for permanent civil engineering works?
bankQuestions.explanation: A good building stone should have a specific gravity greater than 2.6 to ensure density, low porosity, and structural durability.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Good building stone specific gravity should be > 2.6.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: On Mohs Scale of Mineral Hardness, which mineral is assigned a hardness value of 1 (the softest mineral)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Talc is rated 1 on Mohs hardness scale. The full scale: 1 Talc, 2 Gypsum, 3 Calcite, 4 Fluorite, 5 Apatite, 6 Feldspar, 7 Quartz, 8 Topaz, 9 Corundum, 10 Diamond.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Mohs Scale: 1 Talc (softest), 2 Gypsum, 3 Calcite, 7 Quartz, 10 Diamond (hardest).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: On Mohs Scale of Mineral Hardness, which mineral is assigned a hardness value of 10 (the hardest natural substance)?
bankQuestions.explanation: Diamond is assigned the maximum value of 10 on Mohs scale.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Mohs scale hardness 10 = Diamond. Hardness 9 = Corundum. Hardness 7 = Quartz.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does "Smith Test" perform on a stone sample?
options: Detects the presence of soluble, earthy, or muddy matter by shaking fresh stone chippings in clean water in a glass cylinder
bankQuestions.explanation: Smith test detects earthy or clayey impurities: clean stone chippings are shaken with clean water; if water remains clear, stone is durable; if muddy, stone contains clay.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Smith Test = detects soluble/earthy matter by shaking stone chips in clean water.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What does the "Acid Test" assess on a building stone sample?
options: The weathering resistance of sandstone and limestone when exposed to acidic atmospheric fumes and acid rain
The chemical acidity of quarry sap
bankQuestions.explanation: Acid test immerses stone in 1% hydrochloric or sulfuric acid for 7 days to evaluate weather resistance; sharp corners breaking off indicates poor durability.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Acid test assesses resistance of building stones to atmospheric acid weathering.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which machine is standardly used to conduct the Attrition Test on road metal stones to determine their resistance to wear?
bankQuestions.explanation: The Deval Attrition machine rotates 5 kg of stone chippings at 30 rpm for 10,000 revolutions to measure percentage of wear across a 1.5 mm sieve.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Deval machine = Attrition test. Los Angeles machine = Abrasion test.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Quarry Sap" in freshly extracted building stones?
options: The natural moisture held in the pores of freshly quarried stone, making the stone softer and easier to dress before it dries out and hardens
An adhesive resin secreted by tree roots
bankQuestions.explanation: Freshly quarried stone contains internal moisture called quarry sap. Stones are soft and dressed easily while sap is present; drying in air hardens the stone.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Quarry sap is natural moisture in fresh stone; stone is dressed before sap evaporates.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What explosive composition forms standard Black Blasting Powder (Gunpowder) used in quarrying stones where splitting without shattering is desired?
bankQuestions.explanation: Gunpowder (blasting powder) is 75% KNO3 + 15% C + 10% S. It produces a slow heaving explosion that dislodges large building blocks without shattering.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Blasting powder = 75% Potassium Nitrate + 15% Charcoal + 10% Sulfur.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the ideal percentage of Silica (SiO2) in good brick earth, and what is its primary function?
options: 50% to 60%; it prevents raw bricks from shrinking, warping, and cracking during drying and burning
20% to 30%; it provides plasticity for moulding
bankQuestions.explanation: Good brick clay contains 50-60% silica. It preserves the shape of the brick and prevents shrinkage and warping. Excess silica makes bricks brittle.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Silica in brick earth: 50% to 60% (prevents shrinkage, cracking, warping).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the ideal percentage of Alumina (Al2O3) in good brick earth, and what is its primary function?
options: 20% to 30%; it imparts the necessary plasticity required to mould the clay into rectangular brick shapes
5% to 6%; it acts as a flux
bankQuestions.explanation: Alumina constitutes 20-30% of brick earth, providing plasticity. Excess alumina causes bricks to shrink and warp excessively during drying.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Alumina in brick earth: 20% to 30% (provides plasticity for moulding).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What harmful effect occurs in bricks if the raw brick earth contains excess Alumina (greater than 30%)?
options: Raw bricks shrink excessively, develop deep cracks, and warp during drying and burning
Bricks become too brittle and crumble into powder
bankQuestions.explanation: Excess alumina makes the clay overly sticky; upon drying, it shrinks severely, creating cracks and warping.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Excess Alumina causes bricks to shrink, crack, and warp during drying.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the role of Iron Oxide (Fe2O3) present in brick earth in the proportion of 5% to 6%?
options: Imparts the characteristic red colour to finished burnt bricks and acts as a flux fusing silica grains
bankQuestions.explanation: Iron oxide (5-6%) gives burnt bricks their red colour. It also acts as a flux, helping silica fuse at lower temperatures.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Iron oxide (5-6%) imparts red colour and helps fuse silica in bricks.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What harmful effect occurs in finished bricks if the brick earth contains pebbles or nodules of Lime (calcium carbonate)?
options: Upon burning, lime turns to quicklime (CaO), which subsequently slakes upon absorbing atmospheric moisture, expanding and bursting the brick (lime popping / flaking)
bankQuestions.explanation: Lime nodules calcine into quicklime (CaO). Later, moisture causes hydration into Ca(OH)2 with a 2.5x volume expansion that splits the brick.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Lime lumps in brick earth cause lime popping/flaking and bursting upon slaking.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Efflorescence" in burnt clay bricks?
options: The appearance of unsightly white powdery salt deposits on the exposed brick surface caused by the presence of soluble alkalies (sodium and potassium salts)
The fungal rotting of wet bricks
The melting of overburnt brick corners
The fading of brick red colour under sunlight
bankQuestions.explanation: Soluble alkalies in brick earth dissolve in moisture and migrate to the surface as water evaporates, leaving white crystalline salt patches (efflorescence).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Efflorescence = white powdery salt crusts on brick surfaces caused by soluble alkalies.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What machine is standardly employed in brick manufacturing to thoroughly knead, temper, and homogenize the plastic clay paste with water?
bankQuestions.explanation: A Pug Mill is a conical iron tub with rotating radial blades that thoroughly mixes, kneads, and tempers clay and water into plastic moulding earth.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Pug Mill is used for tempering and kneading brick clay.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the standard Modular size of a common burnt clay building brick as specified by the Bureau of Indian Standards (IS 1077)?
options: 190 mm x 90 mm x 90 mm (19 cm x 9 cm x 9 cm)
bankQuestions.explanation: The standard modular dimension of a brick in India is 190 mm x 90 mm x 90 mm (19 x 9 x 9 cm).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Standard Modular brick size = 19 cm x 9 cm x 9 cm (190 x 90 x 90 mm).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the Nominal size of a standard modular brick including a 10 mm mortar joint on all sides?
options: 200 mm x 100 mm x 100 mm (20 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm)
bankQuestions.explanation: With a standard 10 mm mortar joint added, the nominal modular brick size is 200 mm x 100 mm x 100 mm (20 x 10 x 10 cm).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Nominal brick size (with mortar) = 20 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm (200 x 100 x 100 mm).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the indent or depression formed on the top bed face of a hand-moulded brick called, and what is its dual purpose?
options: Frog; it forms a mechanical shear key for mortar bonding and displays the manufacturer brand name
bankQuestions.explanation: The depression (usually 100 x 40 x 10-20 mm) is the Frog. It forms a mortar shear key locking adjacent courses together and displays the maker initials.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Frog (10-20 mm deep) forms a mortar shear key and carries the manufacturer stamp.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the minimum compressive crushing strength required for First Class Bricks under IS 1077?
bankQuestions.explanation: First class bricks must have a minimum compressive strength of 10.5 N/mm² (105 kg/cm²).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Compressive strengths: 1st class ≥ 10.5 N/mm², 2nd class ≥ 7.0 N/mm², 3rd class ≥ 3.5 N/mm².
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the maximum water absorption permitted for First Class Bricks after 24 hours of cold water immersion?
options: Not more than 20% of its dry weight
Not more than 10% of dry weight
Not more than 25% of dry weight
Not more than 5% of dry weight
bankQuestions.explanation: First class bricks should not absorb more than 20% of their dry weight after 24 hours immersion in water (Second class: 22%, Third class: 25%).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Water absorption: 1st class ≤ 20%, 2nd class ≤ 22%, 3rd class ≤ 25%.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What are overburnt, vitrified, dark, irregular, and distorted bricks known as in brick kiln manufacturing?
bankQuestions.explanation: Overburnt vitrified bricks are called Jhama bricks. They are hard, brittle, and out of shape; crushed into ballast for foundation concrete or road sub-base.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Jhama bricks = overburnt, vitrified bricks used as road metal and foundation concrete aggregate.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which continuous brick kiln operates in an oval or circular excavated trench in the ground using movable iron chimneys moved progressively as burning advances?
bankQuestions.explanation: Bull Trench Kiln is a semi-continuous trench kiln where brick loading, drying, burning, cooling, and unloading occur simultaneously in different sections using movable chimneys.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Bull Trench Kiln uses movable chimneys in an excavated trench.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which permanent, circular or elliptical continuous brick kiln features permanent masonry chambers and a tall central stationary chimney?
bankQuestions.explanation: Hoffman kiln is a permanent continuous kiln with a massive brick structure and tall central chimney, highly fuel efficient and producing top-quality bricks.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Hoffman Kiln = permanent continuous kiln with central chimney.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "Queen Closer" in brick masonry?
options: A piece of brick obtained by cutting a standard brick lengthwise into two equal halves (190 mm x 45 mm x 90 mm)
A brick cut across its width into two halves
A brick cut triangularly at the corner
A full brick laid vertically on edge
bankQuestions.explanation: A queen closer is formed by splitting a brick longitudinally along its centerline, producing a piece 190 x 45 x 90 mm, placed next to a quoin header to create lap.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Queen Closer = brick cut LENGTHWISE into two equal halves (190 x 45 x 90 mm).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Where is a Queen Closer specifically placed in a course of brick masonry?
options: Immediately next to the corner Quoin Header to create the necessary vertical joint overlap
At the very end of the wall
At the center of a partition
bankQuestions.explanation: A queen closer is always inserted immediately adjacent to the quoin header (never at the corner itself) to stagger vertical joints in subsequent courses.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Queen closer is placed NEXT to the quoin header.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is a "King Closer" in brick masonry?
options: A piece of brick cut triangularly from the center of one header face to the center of one stretcher face, leaving half-header and half-stretcher intact
A brick cut longitudinally into four pieces
A curved brick for arch construction
bankQuestions.explanation: A king closer is formed by cutting off a triangular corner from mid-header to mid-stretcher, frequently used at door and window jambs.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: King Closer = corner cut from center of header to center of stretcher.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the characteristic arrangement of bricks in "English Bond" brick masonry?
options: Alternate courses of entire stretchers and entire headers, with a queen closer placed next to the quoin header in every header course
Headers and stretchers laid alternately in the same course
All bricks laid as stretchers throughout
bankQuestions.explanation: English bond consists of alternating courses: one course purely of headers, next course purely of stretchers. It is the strongest bond in brick masonry.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: English Bond = alternate courses of headers and stretchers (STRONGEST bond).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the characteristic arrangement of bricks in "Flemish Bond" brick masonry?
options: Every course consists of alternate headers and stretchers laid continuously along the same row
One full course of headers followed by one course of stretchers
Bricks laid diagonally in herringbone patterns
bankQuestions.explanation: In Flemish bond, headers and stretchers alternate within every single course, creating an attractive face appearance with staggered joints.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Flemish Bond = alternate headers and stretchers in the SAME course.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which brick bond is considered structurally the STRONGEST bond for walls of all thicknesses?
bankQuestions.explanation: English bond has no continuous vertical joints and provides maximum structural interlocking, making it stronger than Flemish bond.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: English bond is structurally STRONGER than Flemish bond.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Which brick bond presents a more artistic and aesthetically pleasing face appearance, commonly chosen for exposed face brickwork?
bankQuestions.explanation: Flemish bond produces a balanced, pleasing geometric pattern of alternating headers and stretchers, preferred for decorative face work.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Flemish bond provides better aesthetic appearance than English bond.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Stretcher Bond" (Running Bond), and what is the typical thickness of a wall built using it?
options: All bricks are laid as stretchers along the wall length, producing a half-brick thick wall (100 mm or 10 cm thickness)
All bricks laid as headers with one-brick thickness
bankQuestions.explanation: In stretcher bond, all bricks show their long faces (stretchers). It is restricted to half-brick (100 mm / 10 cm) partition walls and cavity wall leaves.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Stretcher bond builds HALF-BRICK thick walls (10 cm / 100 mm) for partitions.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: Where is "Header Bond" specially employed in brick masonry construction?
options: In curved brick walls where short header faces turn smooth curves without protruding arrises, and in brick footing steps
bankQuestions.explanation: Header bond (all headers) is used for curved brick walls because the shorter 90 mm face follows a curved profile smoothly, and for spreading footing loads.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Header bond is used for curved brick walls and footing load distribution.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Quicklime" chemically, and how is it produced from natural limestone?
options: Calcium Oxide (CaO), produced by the calcination (heating) of limestone to drive off carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
bankQuestions.explanation: Quicklime (caustic lime) is Calcium Oxide (CaO), produced by burning limestone in a lime kiln at 800-900°C to release carbon dioxide gas.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Quicklime = Calcium Oxide (CaO). Calcination: CaCO3 + heat -> CaO + CO2.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the chemical reaction known as "Slaking of Lime"?
options: Adding water to quicklime, converting it into hydrated lime with immense release of heat: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + Heat
bankQuestions.explanation: Slaking is the vigorous exothermic hydration of quicklime: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. The volume expands 2 to 2.5 times with a hissing sound and steam generation.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Slaking: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + Heat (volume expands 2 to 2.5 times).
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: How does pure "Fat Lime" (high-calcium lime) harden and set after application on walls?
options: By absorbing carbon dioxide (CO2) from the surrounding atmospheric air: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O
By reacting with water under submerged conditions
bankQuestions.explanation: Fat lime sets strictly by carbonation—absorbing atmospheric CO2 to reform crystalline calcium carbonate. It cannot set underwater or in damp thick walls devoid of air.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Fat lime sets by carbonation (absorbing CO2 from air); does NOT set underwater.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is "Hydraulic Lime", and what enables it to set and harden under water?
options: Lime containing 5% to 30% clay (silica and alumina) which chemically forms insoluble hydrated calcium silicates underwater without needing air
bankQuestions.explanation: Hydraulic lime contains clay. During burning, silica and alumina combine with lime to form calcium silicates/aluminates that set underwater like cement.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: Hydraulic lime contains clay (5-30%); sets underwater in the absence of air.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to IS 712 classification of building limes, which class represents "Eminently Hydraulic Lime" used for structural masonry and foundations?
bankQuestions.explanation: IS 712 classifies limes into: Class A (Eminently hydraulic, used for structural masonry/foundations), Class B (Semi-hydraulic), Class C (Fat lime for whitewashing).
bankQuestions.rankerTip: IS 712: Class A = Eminently Hydraulic Lime for structural works and foundations.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to IS 712 classification, which class of lime represents "Fat Lime" used specifically for white washing and finishing coat plastering?
bankQuestions.explanation: Class C lime is Fat Lime (rich lime), consisting of high-calcium lime used predominantly for whitewashing and finishing coats of decorative plaster.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: IS 712: Class C = Fat Lime for whitewashing and finishing plaster.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: According to IS 712 classification, which class of lime represents "Semi-Hydraulic Lime" used for general masonry mortar?
bankQuestions.explanation: Class B lime is Semi-hydraulic lime, containing moderate clay content (approx 15%), standardly used for building masonry mortars.
bankQuestions.rankerTip: IS 712: Class B = Semi-hydraulic lime for masonry mortars.
bankQuestions.examName: Kerala PSC Surveyor Gr. II / Land Records

bankQuestions.question: What is the principal chemical oxide present in the highest proportion (60% to 67%) in Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC)?
